We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the graph's weak neighborhood relation, as well as two fixed-parameter algorithms based on duality principles - one using the SPQR tree approach and the other using the layer decomposition technique. Our novel method leverages the SPQR tree approach to provide a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the tree-block decomposition, achieving a comparable run time complexity of O(1.4992^k k^5 m^4). Furthermore, we've established that tree decomposition does not work well for this specific problem, given the known bound of k^ℓ m for a graph with a neighborhood decomposition having a branch width of ℓ. Our research also shows that a parameterized version of the group coloring problem, capable of being solved in O(2.27^k k k^2 m) time, can be used to further reduce the run time complexity of the upward planar drawing algorithms by incorporating the graph's maximum degree as a parameter. However, it's worth noting that a version of the upward planar drawing problem with the graph's neighborhood degree and a specific structure-based parameter - namely, the width of a tree-block decomposition - is computationally infeasible; in contrast, a version of the problem with a specific and more restrictive parameter - namely, the width of a layer decomposition - is also infeasible. Additionally, we've established an O(2.27^k k^3 m^2) time complexity for a parameterized version of the list-orientation problem, capable of being solved in linear time when the graph's maximum degree equals 2. Our research also reveals key insights into previous algorithms and results, explaining their limitations and precision. In particular, a version of the upward planar drawing problem with a parameter of k and a specific constraint - namely, a degree constraint - was previously solved in O(k^7 m^3) time; in contrast, our research demonstrates that a version of the problem with an increased parameter - namely, the square of the maximum degree - along with the degree constraint, is also solvable in O(2.07^k k^5 m^4) time and can be further reduced to O(2.07^k k^2 m^2) time using a version of the problem with an increased parameter - namely, the cube of the maximum degree - that was previously unknown. Crowdsourced image datasets, often marred by noise, pose a significant challenge for even the most sophisticated neural networks. This difficulty arises from class imbalance and uncertainties in labeling, issues that are particularly prevalent in datasets consisting of images of ancient Greek papyri such as AL-PRIVATE. When incorporating uncertainty estimates into the classification process, conventional deep learning models exhibit a notable improvement in accuracy. This article presents a unified framework combining a CNN with uncertainty estimation techniques and a multinomial logistic regression model to classify images, outperforming existing methods with a high degree of confidence. This approach relies on two key methodologies: utilizing Gaussian dropout for generating uncertainty estimates and selecting optimal sample probabilities based on entropy measurements. This methodology was implemented in two stages: initially, the sample images were preprocessed and fed into the combined system for classification; the resulting probability distributions were then calculated and normalized before applying the logistic regression to obtain the final classification outcome. Experimental results demonstrate that this method is capable of successfully classifying noisy images while accounting for distribution shifts. This approach has the potential to benefit a wider range of image classification tasks involving uncertain data. By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure of the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. The discovered phase shift, occurring at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point without magnetic field, can be identified by measuring the stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice, at a doping concentration of $x=p=0.17$. Our theoretical calculations using the Eilenberger theory for interlocked vortices demonstrate that this transition represents the expected rotation of the square lattice structure by 45 degrees predicted for materials that are $d$-wave superconductors near a point of high singularity. As a result, this newly discovered phase shift provides conclusive proof that La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ belongs to the family of $d$-wave superconductors. Furthermore, this unique properties-enhancing effect is expected to induce exceptional properties in other exotic material s in this family. Classifying every video into precise time-stamped action segments is crucial for diverse real-world applications like surveillance. Current solutions rely on extensive annotated datasets but certain approaches suggest that unsupervised methods can produce comparable results by identifying distinct temporal patterns in data. However, prevalent methods often rely on robust signal extraction and fail to address the complexity of mixed action time-series. This paper proposes a novel unsupervised approach, referred to as SSCAP, to determine lengthy, complex action durations. It involves a neural architecture that composes a multi-layer capsule network, sequence learning, and attention mechanisms to simultaneously recognize long and short-lived actions. The model utilizes class activation diagrams in an efficient aggregation strategy that leverages diverse class-specific features, thereby enhancing recognition of mixed actions. Experiments on various action datasets demonstrate the superiority of SSCAP, which outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised methods across multiple evaluation metrics. Additionally, the model shows strong performance when fine-grained annotations are limited. This approach is presented at \url{https://sscap.github.io}. The source code can be accessed at \url{https://sscap.github.io}. 

This study's key contributions include the development of SSCAP, a unsupervised action segmentation method, and the establishment of strong benchmarks on UCF101-25, UFC101, UFC200 and KAGGLE-Surveillance actions. Moreover, the introduction of unsupervised multi-capacity capsule networks, efficient aggregation strategies and the use of class activation diagrams in classifying complex long and short action durations.

Current educational strategies often fail to effectively engage students in the learning process, particularly in the area of testing. In an effort to address this, we sought to design and implement an innovative curriculum aimed at teaching testing concepts to computer science students in a high school setting. By utilizing an inquiry-based method, we created a Learning Inquiry model, which comprised Threats, Bugs, and Fixes. The model utilizes scenario-based assignments and simulates real-world environments, encouraging students to resolve problems posed by their peers. According to student evaluations, the curriculum was found to be engaging and insightful, and we discuss its benefits, challenges, and future development opportunities. Furthermore, we examine the curricula's alignment with industry standards and highlight the importance of involving industrial experts in the development process. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to the discussion on teaching testing and highlight opportunities for improvement in the field. The model's source code and additional resources are accessible via https://github.com/milanei/testing-edu. A educational video illustrating the model's operation can be viewed at https://youtu.be/AU9k1001UDI. 
This curriculum was initially presented at the 21st Annual Research in IT conference in 2021 and has since been refined with fresh outcomes from the same event in 2021.

Domain adaptation has been applied extensively to handle distribution shifts across various fields like vision, language, and multimedia. Most existing domain adaptation techniques leverage domain-invariant features by utilizing both source and target domain data. However, when source data is inaccessible due to privacy concerns, this strategy becomes impractical. To resolve this issue, we propose a novel method that adapts source models via hypothesis transfer without requiring access to source data. This approach involves a semi-supervised learning technique that iteratively utilizes entropy minimization and augmented label propagation for intra-domain and inter-domain alignments. Experimental results on multiple public datasets demonstrate that our proposed method yields significant improvements of up to 19.9% compared to state-of-the-art baseline methods, particularly in semi-supervised adaptation tasks. Additional analysis shows that our proposed technique outperforms existing domain adaptation methods by 5.6% on a recent adaptation task, which was initially handled in a fully supervised setting. The proposed method, code, and datasets are publicly available on GitHub. Furthermore, this work yields another contribution by setting up a novel benchmark dataset for unsupervised visual domain adaptation, named CharactSZ, which utilizes five distinct vision datasets featuring diverse domain shifts and complex characteristics. The datasets are also publicly available at https://github.com/Cpai21/Semi-MUE. The CharactSZ dataset benchmark can serve as a valuable resource for researchers to develop and evaluate domain adaptation methods based on heterogeneous data. This dataset benchmark may also provide insights into novel domain adaptation approaches for real-world applications across various fields. This study presents a novel neural network architecture for particle physics research that leverages localization in time-projection chamber technology for dark matter exploration. Characteristic signals within these TPCs facilitate particle interaction localization via a reconstruction process, making them a focus for multilayer perceptron-based approaches like those using MLPs for reconstruction in TPCs. However, MLPs are a "black-box" method, lacking particle physics expertise and thus failing to effectively use low-resolution data from TPC's detector layers. The proposed Domain-informed Neural Network, DiNN, incorporates domain knowledge in TPC geometry without relying on pixel data from all layers for localization. Instead of a straightforward MLP input, DiNN uses a spatial propagation unique to each layer that informs the final localization and is trainable, as well as utilizing learned weights in each layer, enhancing its adaptive capabilities. When evaluated using detector signals from only two out of six layers, DiNN shows superior performance over MLPs, achieving an average 35% reduction in localization volume. Additionally, DiNN maintains its accuracy in rare event analysis, demonstrating an 84% success rate in locating non-random events, such as dark matter signals, compared to the 74% achieved by MLPs. Since the method utilizes learned weights, it has the additional benefit of being applicable across various types of TPCs, including large and focal plane TPCs. Code for the DiNN architecture is available at the repository https://github.com/next-generation-personnel/DiNN for public access and can be easily integrated into detector signal analysis as an automatic localization tool. As localization is an essential step in particle signal identification, a precise and automated method like DiNN is crucial for signal verification and validation. Furthermore, DiNN has the potential to significantly accelerate analysis and validation in space-based dark matter experiments including X-AMANOGAWA, LUX-Zeplin, and PANDAX. Future variations of DiNN, incorporating particle physics research insights, may also enable predictions based on the analyzed particle interactions, offering additional analysis capabilities. Emerging novel machine learning techniques, like mixed physics research for localization, may further enhance the method's effectiveness and efficiency in particle interactions and identification. Lastly, the use of neural networks for localization offers the advantage of enabling feedback and iteration between localization and identification analysis, a significant benefit. This text offers an in-depth explanation of the theoretical underpinnings of variable instantiation in Answer Set Programming. We build upon ASP's modeling language semantics to define a formal description of grounding algorithms using (fixed point) operators. Central to this are well-established, fixed-point operators providing models that offer semantic insights into the outcome of grounding as well as facilitating simplifications during processing. We address a broad range of logic programs that incorporates recursive aggregates and extends the reach of existing ASP modeling languages, complemented by an algorithmic framework outlining the process of grounding recursive aggregates. These provided algorithms correspond closely to those utilized by the ASP grounder, gringo. We also demonstrate how the foundational theory of ASP's semantics can be leveraged to introduce new algorithmic simplifications that reduce data management during processing. These introduced simplifications originate from the evaluation of aggregates during processing and are applicable even when generators are present. The described algorithms do not generate actual answers but rather provide a fundamental understanding of the outcome of grounding as well as an efficient way to determine whether a logic program can be fully instantiated. These offered theoretical formulations contribute to the creation of grounding algorithms by providing a clear, mathematical description of the algorithmic decisions. Furthermore, this theory facilitates a deeper understanding of the interaction between the grounding algorithm and the type of logic programs being processed, ultimately leading to the development of specialized groupers tailored to particular program patterns or features. As an example of this, we present a dedicated grouper for logic programs utilizing recursive aggregates that reduces data management during processing and is designed to pair well with the ASP solver, asp9.6. A final consideration outlines potential areas for further research regarding the theory of grounding algorithms. These offered theoretical formulations are envisioned to contribute to the ongoing improvement in processing times during Answer Set Programming. All presented implementation details are documented in a companion paper, D. Gelá, L. Pfeiffer. Grounding recursive aggregates. In 25th International Conference on Logic Programming, 2019. We have extended quantum resource theories to encompass complex scenarios with multiple intertwined resources that dictate the behavior of physical systems. By formulating interconversion conditions for these combined resources, we have identified a general method for calculating the relative entropy distances of invariant subsets within a system. This approach enables the tracing out of specific resources, yielding an extended quantum resource theory framework that encompasses diverse physical systems such as thermodynamics, discrete quantum mutiplexing, and multi-qubit entanglement. Furthermore, our framework's resources demonstrate graded invertibility and we show how to manage the degree of invertibility through the introduction of 'hypotheses'. By examining these hypotheses, we have derived necessary and sufficient conditions for the convertibility of pure multiplexed resources and the reversibility of thermodynamic processes. Our analysis also reveals the existence of non-trivial correlations between resources and the crucial nature of their initial forms in enabling transformations, as exemplified by our demonstration that discrete quantum multiplexing resources can't be completely converted from Multipartite entanglement resources, regardless of prior measurements. Lastly, we have developed methods for computing resource fees - the generalization of entropy - in both multiplexing and thermodynamics settings. These fees represent the minimum amount of one resource required to enable the conversion or enable the transformation of another resource. Our analysis reveals the Block-entropy, given by the relative entropy of block-states, as a fundamental component in the fee structure and the entropy production, given by the relative entropy of steady states, as a fundamental component in the block-entropy in thermodynamics, given by the relative entropy of block-states. Our work thus provides a fundamental structure for the free energy landscape in the zero-temperature dQdW process. These results represent significant advancements in the field of quantum resource theories, offering new insights and perspectives. Our papers' appendices provide an in-depth analysis of the interplay between resource theories and Bayesian inference theories. These theories, which govern the behavior of physical systems, apply the principles of objectivity and causality to probability theories, which in turn, provide physical explanations for the behavior of these systems. Our work thus forms the foundational principles of the field of quantum thermodynamics, providing new insights and perspectives. Our papers' appendices explore the relationship between the mathematical concepts of extension and the philosophical ideas of externalism, and show how the former can lead to the latter. Our work thus addresses questions regarding the mathematical and philosophical nature of the field. Recent searches for supersymmetry at the classical level have not provided any conclusive signs of new physics. In response, the CMS is implementing specialized searches aimed at more complex and precise supersymmetry scenarios. This contribution will focus on three new searches using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data recorded with the CMS detector between 2016 and 2018: a heavy gluino search involving the decay of heavy neutralinos and resulting in boosted Z bosons and undetected energy; a search for supersymmetry compression in final states featuring soft tau particles; and an investigation into compressed, long-lived charginos in hadronic final states displaying vanished particle tracks. Each search is discussed in terms of its implementation, results, and future directions. Additionally, the development of these searches is placed in the broader context of the LHC search strategy for supersymmetry. In particular, these new searches are part of a larger effort by the CMS to explore the moderate priority range of the supersymmetry parameter space. In contrast to more traditional supersymmetry searches, these searches are focused on areas of interest from various effective field theory models rather than the original supersymmetry model itself. In the near future, the search program will continue to evolve in response to growing data sets and improving analysis techniques. Furthermore, the use of machine learning is being incorporated into the search program in an effort to refine the separation between signal and background, though this approach is still in its early stages. In general, the search program is being shaped by a balance between covering a diverse range of supersymmetry scenarios and leveraging unique aspects of the data, such as the detection of energy not associated with charged particles. In the event that data is found to contain a signal, the use of reverse searches will help to establish the basis of a physics outcome, including which supersymmetry scenario is responsible. Conversely, the absence of a signal will simply expand the scope of the search program, incorporating additional scenarios and regions of interest in the months and years to come. Ultimately, the effectiveness of the strategy will be judged following fourteen years of operation, during which time the LHC will have completed three distinct runs, each representing a distinct scientific era. Novel view synthesis with light field rendering traditionally achieves accurate reproduction of view-dependent phenomena by densely sampling a scene's views, yet these processes are often computationally expensive. In contrast, geometric reconstruction methods only require sparse views but often struggle to replicate non-Lambertian light interactions. Our new model strikes a balance by learning view-dependent effects in four-dimensional light field space and inferring scene geometry from sparse views using different neural operators. Additionally, we introduced an attentional fusion module to combine geometry and light field cues effectively. At the core of our method, the Attentionable Four-dimensional Light Field Model (AFLM) efficiently decomposes a scene into stationary components, including geometry and light, across multiple epochs. Our approach therefore successfully synthesizes novel views while efficiently detecting and generating view-dependent and independent elements. Evaluations using synthetic and real-world datasets confirm our approach's superior performance over state-of-the-art baselines. Further implementation details and code are available online. Moreover, our work demonstrates the effectiveness of four-dimensional representation in synthesizing novel views accurately and efficiently. Our results suggest that most real-world scenes can rely on combining sparse geometry and light field features to accurately reproduce appearances. Therefore, our approach's design as a sum of geometric and light field terms is optimal for synthesizing views in non-Lambertian scenes without requiring dense views. Our contribution to view synthesis as a four-dimensional representation learning process opens up avenues for further research along this dimension, including the application of our code to other benchmark datasets and the extension of our approach to address novel tasks such as occlusion matting in novel view synthesis. A powerful and dynamic solar eruption triggered by shock waves emanating from the Sun's corona can accelerate electrons, resulting in the formation of type II radio bursts. Although such bursts have been observed in various solar phenomena, including solar imprints and filaments, their origin remains unclear, particularly as they do not seem to stem from the sources of coronal mass ejections. Our study presents the first documentation of a type II radio burst originating from a growing solar filament. A unique radio burst was detected on October 10, 2015, showing characteristics typical of type II radio bursts. Its association with a developing filament rather than a coronal mass ejection or streamer on the same solar structure suggests that the electron acceleration responsible for the burst may have been triggered by the increasing magnetic field and/or increasing density of the solar structure. As the burst's speed exceeded the average speed of coronal mass ejections, it is proposed that the electron acceleration could have been further enhanced by a process of relativastical acceleration. Balancing communication efficiency and data privacy is a critical concern in distributed neural network training. To address this gap, we have created an innovative approach that reconciles the requirements of efficient communication and differential privacy. We integrated Relative Entropy Coding, a highly efficient compression technique, into the distributed training framework. By introducing a simple adjustment to REC, we derived a differential privacy compliant algorithm, which provides quantifiable guarantees. Experimental results show that our approach substantially decreases communication costs while maintaining high data privacy standards. Moreover, we found that the proposed method achieves higher compression ratios compared to existing methods and offers superior data privacy assurances. To further enhance the privacy properties, we have also developed a meta-algorithm that leverages the properties of Relative Entropy Coding and the data privacy guarantee provided by the SMPC framework. This meta-algorithm can provide more stringent data privacy guarantees at no initial cost, but incurs higher compression costs to obtain better privacy. The proposed methods and frameworks are open-source and available on GitHub, contributing to a better understanding of the trade-offs between communication costs, data privacy, and compression costs in distributed neural network training. This research aims to address the emerging field of privacy-preserving machine learning. Over the past ten years, substantial advancements have taken place to minimize the occurrence of incorrect positive results in data retrieval systems. Nevertheless, established solutions may not be optimal for situations that involve retrieving data items that are not only infrequently accessed but also highly sensitive in nature. In light of this, there is a pressing need for systems that effectively contain the spread of these sensitive items. To address this issue, we propose the development of a Cyclic Filter Structure (CFS) that not only significantly lowers the occurrence of incorrect positive results but also prevents the exposure of sensitive data to unauthorized parties through a mechanism that ensures cyclic data circulation. Furthermore, we introduce three distinct types of cyclic filter prototypes, namely the Cyclic Cuckoo Filter, Cyclic Dense Filter, and Cyclic Element Filter, that cater to different memory usage scenarios. Our experimental findings demonstrate that these proposed structures not only contain the spread of sensitive data but also achieve competitive, if not superior, performance characteristics when compared to existing filtering mechanisms. Our solutions have far-reaching implications as they offer the first tangible solution to contain the spread of sensitive items while ensuring optimal data retrieval performance. Additionally, we achieve a 21% suppression in the occurrence of incorrect positive results in real-world use cases without compromising the overall performance. Our experimental findings and source code are publicly available on https://github.com/uiwbj/cyclic-filter-structures. A shift towards using quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to classical processing. We develop and test a quantum-inspired machine learning technique that effectively recognizes nonlinear patterns in datasets using just a linear number of operations, without requiring advanced quantum computing capabilities. Our approach, implemented on a superconducting quantum processor, successfully categorizes binary images and accurately forecasts the behavior of complex systems, thus marking the first successful completion of a quantum-inspired learning task on a practical quantum computing device. This research focuses on solving spatiotemporal reasoning challenges in object-based video analysis, where prevailing methods lack the ability to comprehend object persistence across different locations in a video frame. Our proposed approach, called BESpaced, makes informed decisions about objects that may have moved to different regions of the video. By incorporating an enhanced object feature representation that captures both intra-frame (features of the same object in different frames) and inter-frame (features of the same frame), BESpaced outperforms current methods on popular video benchmarks. Furthermore, we investigated methods to evaluate machine learning performance on video analysis using both human-based and machine-based assessment techniques, including an analysis of a newly introduced benchmark focusing on object transience. Interestingly, while current models exhibit impressive capabilities in evaluating objects that persist in a specific location, they underperform when it comes to objects that change location, highlighting the importance of further research in this area. The full implementation of our method is available at https://github.com/alex1610/Bespaced. Our work aims to advance the development of new techniques that can effectively process object-based video data with varying levels of object persistence. As machine learning advances, our hope is that future systems will not only surpass current performance but also increase our understanding of multi-step reasoning and object persistence in different locations. Ultimately, our goal is to build a more robust learning platform that addresses critical challenges in artificial intelligence. The research paper detailing our findings can be viewed at arXiv:2307.14022. Our team envisions a future where future systems learn to tackle the challenges of object persistence in different locations, thereby increasing our understanding of multi-step reasoning and object persistence in general. While quantum gravitational effects generally break global symmetries, their presence may hold significant value in understanding both particle physics and cosmology. Discovering well-maintained global symmetries could provide a valuable insight into the properties of gravity. A statistically significant detection of cosmic birefringence in the Cosmic Microwave Background may signify a previously undiscovered, though spontaneously broken, global symmetry in nature. A potential explanation for this phenomenon would be a light axion-like particle, the collective effects of which from the early universe could explain the observed birefringence. The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to empower deep neural networks (DNNs) with the ability to draw from past experiences like humans. This capability is referred to as knowledge transferability. Typically, the process of DTL begins by initially training DNNs on general knowledge and then utilizing them for specific tasks through a refinement process called fine-tuning. There have been two commonly observed patterns of transferability among pre-trained DNNs: one being that larger gaps between pre-training data and downstream information result in lower transferability and another indicating that transferability greatly varies between different tasks. Unfortunately, current approaches to measuring knowledge transfer in DNNs are overly simplistic, leading to confusing implications and unclear conclusions. To rectify this, we suggest a new metric that evaluates the combined influence of a dataset's similarity and complexity on the transferability of a pre-trained DNN. This new metric views transferability as a balance between similarity and complexity and recognizes that similarity enhances transferability while complexity hinders it. Additionally, the proposed metric reveals that this interaction between similarity and complexity can either aid or hinder transferability. This concept is applied to GANs (generative adversarial networks) as well as traditional backpropagation-based models, establishing theoretical relationships between these models and their transferability. Ultimately, the findings from this approach support existing theories and provide empirical evidence of their validity. Additionally, the theoretical relationships allow for the development of a predictive model that defines the boundary between good and poor transferability based on the similarity and complexity of the dataset. Lastly, the proposed metric offers an understanding of how to enhance the overall boundary between good and poor transferability, suggesting that it is possible to improve the entire spectrum of transferability by leveraging pre-training data with lower complexities and higher similarities. This provides developers with valuable insights for utilizing pre-trained models more effectively. The findings from the theoretical approach were tested on a variety of English and non-English NLP tasks to further support its validity. The discovery of the positive interaction between similarity and complexity in transferability has significant implications for pre-training data selection methods, leading to the proposed of Seldap, a new data selection method that targets complexity while preserving similarity to optimize the transferability of pre-trained models. We address this gap by providing an in-depth analysis, through computational methods and statistical modeling, of how division within a network affects information spreading in social systems. Our study reveals that the efficiency of information diffusion greatly depends on the internal structural features of the network, even when the probability of a user accepting information remains relatively consistent. This, in turn, has implications for understanding the spread of diseases and infectious diseases. Our findings also suggest that networks with tightly connected communities make information sharing more efficient, contrary to expectations. Furthermore, our results indicate that the efficiency of a cascade generally decreases as users become increasingly aware of their connections and the internal structural features of the network, regardless of its size or division features. This trade-off between the structural features of a network and the visibility of its internal structures highlights the need to carefully consider the trade-offs between these factors in the design of systems that facilitate information sharing, to ensure optimal diffusion efficiency. Finally, our analysis confirms that the structural features of a network can be valuable indicators of human behavior and should be considered when constructing models to forecast the spread of diseases and infectious diseases. The widespread adoption of Android as the global leading operating system makes it an appealing target for malware. To counter this threat, security experts continuously develop new detection systems based on machine learning, only for malicious attackers to adapt by modifying their malware in various ways. In the field of Android malware evolution research, our work focuses on analyzing problem-space evasion attacks that utilize specific techniques such as character encoding, to avoid being detected by relevant detectors. We selected 13 of these attacks for our analysis and found that 9 of them are still effective in evading detection. We examined the underlying reasons for this through our expertise in natural language processing, revealing important factors such as the alteration of specific characters and sentences used in requests. We also discovered that a significant 64.0% of existing research focuses on general machine learning algorithms, highlighting a knowledge gap in this area. Our work provides insights for researchers to develop more advanced detection systems and better understand the challenges associated with problem-space evasion attacks. Furthermore, our suggested features and validation framework can assist in creating robust security for Android apps that are resilient against these types of attacks. In particular, our study contributes a template-driven API call dataset, useful for researchers to categorize problems associated with specific detectors. We propose a new framework called EviCheak, designed to automatically identify and diagnose problem-space evasion attacks against Android apps. Utilizing this framework, our analysis found that out of 1,525 Android apps examined,  322 are vulnerable to at least one identified evasion attack, while  214 of these apps have never been exposed to an evasion attack, as specified in relevant literature. Additionally, our analysis reveals that vulnerable apps consistently have a lower density of relevant features compared to non-vulnerable apps. In fact, our results specify that apps with a given feature density above 0.15 are 2.63 times more likely to be attacked by a problem-space evasion problem compared to those with a given feature density below 0.15. Our work also demonstrates the efficacy of various machine learning algorithms in detecting evasion attacks, recommending the use of Weighted Subgraph Matching. Our analysis further suggests that developing instance-specific features can provide better detection, allowing us to develop a corresponding model that achieves a PR-AUC of 0.99 using our developed features. Our work includes an automatic diagnosis function, demonstrating its effectiveness in diagnosing 112 real instances of problem-space evasion attacks that were previously overlooked in literature, showcasing its practical applications in testing and verifying the resilience of Android apps against these types of attacks. In the past, the notion of services centered around the exchange of information for compensation, but today services are seen as self-contained components exposing defined operations. This shift in perspective has spawned a variety of service creation and management tools, making it easier to construct services even when the underlying business logic is intricate. Nevertheless, the overwhelming choice of technological platforms and toolkits is making service creation and deployment more challenging, as the lack of standardization creates barriers to accessing customer base, talent, and operational expertise. By defining guidelines for service execution, the generation of RESTful service interfaces, and the formatting of asynchronous response messages, this framework aims to provide a consistent base for various implementation methods. Furthermore, the use of code snippets in this proposal underscores the potential to facilitate human-understandable coding by enabling developers to utilize established services as ready-made components. By combining optimization and information theoretical insights, we demonstrate that when the time and memory costs of the algorithm are taken into account, simple symmetric objective functions can be learned with a significantly smaller number of model parameters than previously thought, under certain conditions. These conditions include having a bounded input dimension, a bounded model width, and a bounded snippet size. A similar result can be applied to Boolean circuits. Additionally, we propose a lower bound for the snippet size based on the concept of mutual information and demonstrate that this bound is not significantly increased by using the multi-task approach. Furthermore, we speculate that speeding up optimization might facilitate discovering compact representations, which could be crucial for tackling even more complex problems. Consequently, research into efficient algorithms may be indispensable for uncovering the intrinsic minimum number of model parameters required to perform a given task. To remain competitive, ridepooling services must balance high pool participation rates against minimizing detours for users. We propose a Branch-and-Cut algorithm to find optimal solutions, utilizing lower and upper bounds that leverage axis-parallelogram cuts and a reduced round-trip travel time objective. To expand upon limited existing solutions, our algorithm allows for the computation of lower bounds through the rapid detection of feasible solutions, and can be paired with pre- and post-processing techniques to extend its limitations further. We tested our approach using a modified version of the Houston instances from the Li et al. collection, and our results show significant improvement for small instances and a substantial reduction in makespan for all cases. For cases of medium to high size, our algorithm consistently finds optimal solutions that previous methods could only approximate. This approach also frequently outperforms general-purpose solvers in terms of computational efficiency. We analyzed the properties of the obtained solutions and found that our algorithm's decision programming model has a high level of integrality for the proposed problem. Additionally, our algorithm's key feature is its ability to exploit problem-specific characteristics and perform well even on challenging problem instances that previous studies could not effectively solve. We also discovered several instances of optimal solutions that reveal the inherent characteristics of the problem. Specifically, our algorithm's design allows it to find valid paths for the case when a customer's destination is a single location, a property that our approach can exploit to find optimal solutions with reduced computational requirements. We performed these experiments and our results show that our algorithm performs well in this context. This study explores multi-modal pretraining techniques for product data in E-commerce, addressing limitations in current methods which struggle with noisy label problems or require significant memory usage. To address these issues, we present LMKD, a novel pretraining framework that combines visual, auditory, and textual information to create a unified modal fusion representation. To differentiate our method from existing research, we introduce two innovative concepts: using modal-specific noise reduction and implementing a unified fusion learning with cross-modal negative sampling. These strategies enable LMKD to effectively remove noisy auditory modal data and learn effective fusion functions without relying on large amounts of purchase data. Through experiments on two large E-commerce product datasets, we demonstrate LMKD's superiority to state-of-the-art models of product modal fusion in terms of quality. Additionally, we utilize the learned representations to enhance our proprietary E-commerce product search engine, achieving significant quality improvements and a 12.2% increase in sales. In conclusion, our research provides a reliable solution for pretraining and deploying modal fusion learning in E-commerce businesses. To facilitate future research, we are releasing our datasets and model code through a public GitHub repository. https://github.com/meituan LTD/LMKD-Code. Note: This study has been accepted at NeurIPS 2022, and won the Best Paper award.

In this research, we investigate whether these standard analyses adequately capture the relevant cosmological information. To address this, we directly fitted synthetic Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions, including cross-correlations with quasars, without compressing the data, and then compared the results to the conventional method. Our approach provided significantly more precise measurements, constraining the matter density to 3.5% and outperforming the conventional BAO method. Our study showed that the additional information, except for the spectral index constraint, came primarily from two distinct effects: the Alcock-Paczy\'nski effect and redshift space distortion. To take full advantage of these new constraints, we suggested combining the Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions with other observations through the standard analysis of galaxy data, enabling the further improvement of precision in measuring the matter density and curvature of the universe. Our work also enabled the detection of non-linear magnification effects in the Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions, revealing a threshold for approximately $10^{-5}$. The refined model used in this research placed no additional statistical requirements on the Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions, facilitating the measurement of the Ly$\alpha$ monopole and bispectrum. Our estimates for the Ly$\alpha$ monopole were consistent with a power-law model of constant flux, while the bispectrum showed a non-random correlation pattern, and our model was able to detect an edge effect in the Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions at approximately $10^1$ Mpc$^{-1}$. The code used for this research, including the analysis tool, is available online. Our work lay the groundwork for future utilization of comprehensive Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions, extending beyond BAO analysis to more in-depth research on the cosmic matter and background radiation properties. This research aims to compare and contrast these measures objectively by exploring their core similarities, disparities, and limitations. To achieve this, a Boltzmann machine architecture is employed as a reference model to analyze how system complexity evolves in response to variations in network dynamics and parameters. Furthermore, a variant of an information-based measure of complexity is applied to examine the process of incremental Hebbian learning in Hopfield networks, which mimic autoassociative memory through a fully recurrent structure. As the network learns to recognize patterns, total information flow consistently increases, mirroring an intrinsic growth in complexity. Conversely, when the network fails to recognize these patterns due to excessive noise, the same measure of complexity reaches its maximum. Notably, this complexity peak coincides with a transient state characterized by high network activity and frequent updates. This transient state represents a critical moment in the learning process, marked by a significant increase in complexity prior to a stable state that embodies lower complexity due to reduced network activity and decreased information flow. Various measures of complexity, albeit with differing definitions, have been applied to this scenario: Zel'dovich, Shreeram Shankar, Komlos, and Peierls measures, all of which show agreement in relation to complexity. Ultimately, an integrated discussion on these metrics in relation to our findings in recurrent neural networks (RNNs) as well as other systems is presented. The choice of RNNs as the primary model for this analysis is based on their widespread applications across scientific disciplines, notably physics, computer science, and neuroscience, as well as the ease with which their architecture can be analyzed symmetrically. This research proposes a comprehensive review of the theoretical underpinnings and a practical examination of the interconnectedness of different complexity measurement approaches. The results of this study demonstrate that constraints in measurement precision may influence the apparent direction of change in complexity depending on the specific measurement used, despite inherent differences in definition. As the precision increases, the results show consistency in complexity for all measures examined, whereas decreased precision leads to conflicting results. Lastly, a theoretical discussion on the nature and significance of time dependence in complexity within RNNs is presented, with the option of integrating additional measurement approaches in future analyses. The accuracy of speech-based applications heavily relies on high-quality speech data. Although existing datasets provide valuable resources for English and German text-based applications, they are limited in their application to automatic speech recognition. To bridge this gap, a comprehensive dataset consisting of spoken articles from the Wikipedia website has been created, featuring speeches in German and English. This resource encompasses articles from diverse domains, including science, sports, art, and more. Analyzing this data reveals significant differences in the content and structure of English and German articles, including distinct distributions, sentence lengths, and the use of special characters. Consequently, English models cannot effectively transcribe German speech, and vice versa. To overcome this limitation, we combined the Spoken Wikipedia Corpus with the Spoken German Corpus to enhance German acoustic models and tested their performance using Kaldi and PyTorch frameworks. Notably, augmenting the data with the Spoken Wikipedia Corpus led to consistent improvements, ranging from 2.3 to 6.6 characters per sentence. While the PyTorch framework yielded slightly better results, the Kaldi framework performed slightly worse with the Spoken Wikipedia Corpus data. These findings suggest that the Spoken Wikipedia Corpus is a valuable resource for refining German acoustic models, and its wide range of domains ensures accurate recognition of domain-specific terms. Overall, we recommend incorporating the Spoken Wikipedia Corpus into existing datasets to enhance the precision of speech-based applications. Deep neural networks, known for their robust performance across various tasks, are often difficult to understand. This interpretability issue severely hampers their use in critical areas like medical imaging. A promising approach to addressing this challenge involves approximate inference with simple, easy-to-interpret submodels. We propose a novel, closed-form reinforcement learning method to learn such submodels that can be used alongside an existing neural network for making predictions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm by achieving state-of-the-art classification accuracy on two medical imaging datasets. Moreover, our method surpasses alternative techniques in one of these datasets by a significant margin. We show that a linear model trained using our method not only rivals but in some cases outperformed a more complex neural network model composed of 8 convolutional layers. We believe our method, which enables scalable and efficient black-box exploration of parameter spaces, has vast potential for making deep neural networks more reliable and understandable. We also anticipate that our method may have applications in explaining and making neural networks more reliable in general. Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We conducted an in-depth analysis of correlated non-Hermitian systems and discovered that correlations cause a significant shift in the topological classification from PT symmetry-based Z2 for non-interacting systems to a Z type of classification for interacting systems. We observed the emergence of a new topological phase with a pair of complex Dirac cones and applied boson-fermion coupling to realize this phase. We further revealed that the correlation's presence erases the subwapping symmetry, causing the sublattices' symmetry distinction to disappear, while the sublattices' individual fermion numbers remain unchanged. Moreover, we established a general topological and symmetry classification for interacting non-Hermitian systems, which will serve as a primary reference for studying correlated topological phases in (1+1) dimensions. Our work provides new avenues for investigating topological phenomena in complex systems. Ultimately, our study may inspire novel ideas for realizing topological phases through boson-fermion interactions and serves as a valuable resource for future research into topological interactions. The research may be extended to (2+1) dimensions to shed light on the effects of interactions on topological systems. A new superdeterministic theory of quantum mechanics known as Invariant-set theory is being proposed. This idea brings concepts from the study of chaotic systems into the field of quantum foundations. Despite quantum mechanics being able to explain many classical phenomena as a lower-level theory, the opposite has yet to happen on a large scale. This suggested theory incorporates two key elements from the study of chaotic systems: measure-preserving maps and the presence of invariant sets. These components allow for the retention of the standard quantum mechanics framework, including its predictions for general situations, while still accommodating the possibility of the predicted Bell correlations to occur. This is achieved by incorporating two distinct notions of states, analogous to the concept of both configuration and velocity in the study of chaotic systems. Furthermore, the theory suggests that quantum mechanics, when viewed in this context, can be seen as behaving in a non-random and pattern-following manner in accordance with a specific principle known as the Kolmogorov-Hopf theorem. This theory also sheds light on why quantum mechanics is able to accurately describe itself and its associated statistics by explaining it as resulting from our limited knowledge of the more fundamental super-quantum theory, similar to how Newton's first law explains the limited applicability of the law "a body at rest remains undisturbed" due to the presence of other forces. In this theory's framework, states are seen as incorporating all the relevant information needed, including the presence of invariant sets, to explain observed phenomena accurately. This theory also has an interesting implication in the context of another concept from the study of chaotic systems known as the phenomenon of resonance, to the extent that it can apply to the dynamics of individual particles. This idea is being proposed as a more elegant alternative to the superdeterministic idea that seeks to contradict the results of Bell's work, with the knowledge that individual particles exhibiting non-local behavior cannot exist in a non-relativistic setting. This means that when we discuss relativistic settings, another beautiful connection arises between the study of chaotic systems and quantum field theory. This is because in the study of chaotic systems, the phenomenon of resonance is known to cause significant changes to the standard dynamics of particles, and this idea suggests that it could cause a similar conflict with the results of Bell's work in the relativistic setting of quantum field theory. This is an area that needs to be explored in more detail, to understand how the study of chaotic systems is connected to the study of quantum field theory. We focus on keyword spotting for IoT devices, requiring minimal computation and power. Deep learning techniques, specifically convolutional neural networks (CNN), have seen significant progress in recent years. This work develops an efficient CNN architecture, dubbed FCNN, by incorporating keyword detection into a two-stage framework. First, we use frequency-magnitude concatenation to enhance keyword representation. Then, we design the CNN structure with lightweight characteristics, including Squeeze-and-Excitation for channel attention, 1D convolution for feature extraction, and 1D max pooling with adaptive thresholding for inference. Additionally, we prune the CNN to reduce parameters and provide theoretical power consumption and inference time estimates. Our results on the Google Speech Dataset show the FCNN achieves an accurate 93.73% recognition rate at 2.53 milliseconds and a power consumption rate of 55.76 milliwatts. The FCNN source code is available at https://github.com/zhuwangpu/FCNN. This includes a detailed implementation of (i) frequency-magnitude concatenation to improve keyword representation, (ii) CNN structure design, and (iii) network pruning. Furthermore, we achieve state-of-the-art performance of 94.22% recognition rate at 2.51 milliseconds and 43.13 milliwatts on the Google Speech Dataset with a more iterative pruning strategy, FCNN*. This implementation demonstrates a 4.718.10 times reduction in power consumption while maintaining 93.73% accuracy without retraining when switching speech datasets. In particular, it successfully transfers from the Google Speech Dataset to the Google Drive Wake Word Dataset and outperforms the benchmark tool in this new environment. Therefore, FCNN serves as a powerful and efficient keyword spotting method for IoT devices with a minimal computational footprint of 0.21 million floating point operations, 0.25 million floating point operations, and 0.53 kilobytes memory usage for power consumption, inference time, and memory footprint respectively. This implies a low communication cost when deploying the FCNN to devices. Furthermore, it has a communication cost of 120 bytes at most in infrastructure. Our results show the FCNN achieves 89.21% relative improvement in power efficiency as compared to the CNN baseline while maintaining a similar accuracy. Similarly, it attains 67.54% relative improvement in inference time and 67.54% relative improvement in memory usage as compared to the CNN baseline while maintaining a similar power consumption rate. The infinite product of determinants, which corresponds to the original Dirac partition function, can then be expressed through the expansion of a finite trigonometric polynomial. In recent years, the needs of embedded systems have grown more complex.  These systems not only require reliable, hard real-time capabilities but also diversified functions like network capabilities.  Implementing virtualization using hypervisors has emerged as a suitable solution to address these demands.  Unfortunately, existing hypervisors, which were designed with general-purpose computing in mind, come with high overhead that is not suitable for embedded systems.  Specifically, the T-Visor hypervisor, which is widely considered an advanced virtualization framework, can still cause substantial performance degradation in mixed criticality embedded systems.  This paper presents a new scheduling framework that is designed specifically to improve the real-time performance of such systems by enhancing the scheduling capabilities of the T-Visor hypervisor.  In contrast to guest-driven scheduling techniques that can lead to poor resource management, the proposed solution employs host-driven scheduling.  This approach leverages the concept of resource partitions to assign CPU resources to guest virtual machines.  A novel scheduling framework known as HHCS, which is based on priority-driven and fixed multiprocessor scheduling, is developed to schedule these resource partitions effectively.  Experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed solution are presented.  These include a product evaluation of HHCS and T-Visor and a comparative analysis of hard real-time performance among different scheduling frameworks.  Our research finds that the proposed scheduling framework can achieve satisfactory and 100% achievable jitter even under adverse scheduling scenarios, thus making it suitable for a variety of embedded system applications.  Moreover, the proposed solution has the potential to be easily adapted to other scheduling frameworks and thus has broad applicability.  In addition to its scheduling capabilities, the paper also explores the impact of context switching on the performance of the hypervisor and proposes optimization strategies to enhance the performance of the framework when subject to context switching.  These optimization techniques involve host-driven and guest-driven context switching scheduling.  Our research finds that the proposed scheduling framework can reduce the number of context switches from guest to host and host to guest, thus enabling better performance under adverse scheduling conditions.  In contrast to guest-driven scheduling techniques that can lead to poor resource management, the proposed scheduling framework effectively schedules context switches from host to guest and host to guest, thus ensuring resource fairness and transparency.  Our research findings reveal that the proposed scheduling framework can reduce the second-order jitter caused by context switching at a factor of nine on average. We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust and adaptable when dealing with slight environmental variations. Building upon the concept from PILCO, a method for probabilistic policy search, our research demonstrates that constraining the uncertainty in the Gaussian Process model's dynamics has a beneficial effect on policy updates and results in more resilient controllers. In addition, our findings highlight the practical advantages of this approach in a simulation-based evaluation. The majority of Reinforcement Learning methods are typically divided into model-free and model-based categories. Model-based methods generally offer better performance but are hindered by their lack of robustness due to any deviations from their learned model. To address this, our research focuses on a probabilistic approach that uses a Gaussian Process dynamic model to guide policy updates and maintain both performance and robustness. This is achieved by setting an upper limit on the uncertainty in the dynamic model, using a metric that measures state properties, to ensure a reliable prediction of the system's behavior. Our simulation-based evaluation, employing the Inverted Pendulum system, showcases the robustness and adaptability of our method by simulating minor changes to the system's dynamics. The results show that our approach successfully avoids failures when the environmental changes were minor, but the controller did act optimally when the changes were more substantial. This resilience was attributed to the controller's ability to withstand uncertainty in the dynamic model and update itself effectively. Our evaluation also reveals that our method surpasses PILCO in both performance and robustness and demonstrates a substantial improvement in performance compared to other methods, showcasing its effectiveness. Furthermore, our method's computational complexity and other practical implications were considered and evaluated, revealing that our method boasts computational efficiency comparable to PILCO and a low memory requirement. To facilitate further research and implementation, our code is openly available online. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that our method offers an advantageous trade-off between performance, robustness, and adaptability, making it an excellent choice for real-world applications that demand these characteristics. Although our focus was on a Gaussian Process dynamic model, our research postulates that our findings can be extended to other probabilistic dynamic models as long as they provide a reliable prediction of the system's behavior. To verify this, our method was applied to a probabilistic dynamic model that used a mixture of Gaussian distributions to model uncertainties in the Balloon Inflation system, further validating our hypothesis. Research in holographic theories reveals a duality between reflected entropy and entanglement wedge cross-sectional area.  Building upon this concept, a similar duality is demonstrated using random tensor networks.  By examining random tensor networks, a sudden increase in reflected entropy through the page phase transition is detected.  By applying a perturbation theoretical approach, this sudden increase's origin can be explained by the resonance of a specific frequency.  The amplitude of this resonance represents the difference in entropy, and its real part corresponds to the difference in entanglement depth.  The imaginary part experiences a decrease as time progresses.  The frequency of the resonance is found to be inversely related to the entanglement wedge cross-sectional area.  These findings validate the concept that reflected entropy measures entanglement depth.  The development of a simple model to calculate reflected entropy allows for the prediction of reflected entropy's real part's relationship with temperature at high temperatures.  The proposed model yields a width of order $1/\sqrt{H\tau}$ for the resonance, indicating the influence of the entanglement wedge cross-sectional area's fluctuation during the page phase transition.  The study concludes with an analysis of the differences between random tensor networks and the holographic setup, revealing under-differentiation in the network model which needs to be addressed for further comparison with the holographic setup's results.  Potential next steps for further research have also been identified.  The study proposes that the development of more sophisticated network models could help to address several mysteries remaining in the field of holographic theories such as the nature of information loss and the origins of holographic entanglement entropy's scaling laws.  The study concludes by identifying several related problems that could be explored using the network model, such as the effects 1. page phase transition at high temperatures 2. wormholes 3. null hypersurface dynamics 4. local operators dynamics.  The study identifies that the abstract concept of entropy is more fundamental than entropy's definition, allowing for the development of different definitions of entropy, such as reflected entropy and holographic entanglement entropy.  The study concludes by identifying a difference between random tensor networks' simplicity and the relatively high complexity of the abelian lattice model compared to the non-abelian lattice model.  The study proposes that the network model's simplicity could help to identify the origins of holographic entanglement entropy's scaling laws, while the non-abelian lattice model's higher complexity may allow for the detection of the roots of several conjectures and mysteries

As an example, the amplitudes for P-wave charmonia mesons are studied, utilizing QCD sum rules to establish a model for the universal function specific to this meson type. In metric geometry and general relativity, specifically Einstein's vacuum equations, generalized differential forms play a significant role. They involve a metric, whose geometric significance is well-established, as a type of generalized vector field. Research into these entities includes studies of their local structure, specifically degeneration into a graded nilpotent Lie algebra with a natural metric, and associated Einstein conditions. Similarly, generalized differential forms appear in the study of Kahler-Riemannian manifolds with torsion, where they represent a type of symmetric tensor field. Similarities between these areas of study highlight their commonalities and encourage further research into the most general scenarios of Einstein metric geometries. This paper explores these concepts further by applying a Lie algebraic framework to the study of metric geometries via their underlying Lie algebras. This approach offers a significant extension of previous work focused on graded Lie algebras. We demonstrate the applicability of this framework to the study of Einstein vacuum equations, generalized Kahler-Riemannian manifolds with torsion, and conformal structures on graded Lie algebras through the introduction of natural Riemannian metrics on $E^\ast$, suitable for decomposition theorems. Furthermore, all results can be generalized to the corresponding cohomology theory. We anticipate that these results will contribute substantially to the study of Einstein metric geometries and broader metric geometry fields. Moreover, the results regarding Einstein conditions will degenerate into unique and unexplored conditions of conformal Einstein metric geometries, previously discussed in the literature. We begin by exploring the Lie theoretical implications of the vacuum condition in a metric geometry, revealing commonalities between this condition and the Kahler-Riemannian condition with torsion. We establish that these conditions are distinct and investigate their potential degeneration into the more fundamental graded Lie algebraic structure. We examine four distinct Einstein conditions derived directly from the metric geometry, as well as two conditions derived from the associated differential forms, in addition to the condition represented by the curvature tensor. We decompose the metric geometry into a graded Lie algebraic structure, characterized by specific Lie algebraic properties, such as metrizable nilpotency. We extend these findings to the broader context of metric geometries by applying the Lie algebraic framework to the study of Einstein vacuum equations, generalized Kahler-Riemannian manifolds with torsion, and conformal structures on graded Lie algebras. We demonstrate the applicability of this framework to the study of Einstein metric geometries via their underlying Lie algebras

diagnostic tools. We have investigated the effectiveness of a simple, low-cost
system that utilizes a combination of images and machine learning for the automatic

91.66% on a further testing dataset of 633 images. The system showed exceptional
ability to detect the presence of parasites when images were sub-standard in
quality or only contained very few parasites. The proposed system has significant
potential to improve the detection of intestinal parasites in low-resource

Typically, investigators either examine the behavior of a single individual within a network or study network communities with a much larger size range, but these approaches fall short of examining the critical process of epidemic spread at a fine-scale level. In order to address this limitation, researchers from the University of Oxford, working with The Alan Turing Institute, utilized high-performance computing to simulate an outbreak on a network of 13 million individuals in the UK, and analyzed yet larger networks with 16 million individuals. By simining an epidemic on a network divided into 300 to 1000 population-sized groups, these studies capture a balance between detailed individual behavior and community effects that cannot be achieved in standard network studies. The maximum likelihood estimator used in CMB map-making provides optimal, unbiased maps, but is influenced by model errors stemming from assumptions about noise and sky signal characteristics. Consideration of these errors involves evaluating the likelihood distribution in the presence of imperfect modeling, which is typically more restrictive than the noise distribution. By taking into account the additional constraints related to the noise distribution, a refined estimator can be developed and contrasted with the two primary alternatives to the maximum likelihood estimator: the two and four data sampling schemes. Despite their names, these schemes do not exactly correspond to sampling under the two and low variance, four data scenarios, respectively. By acknowledging the additional constraints related to the noise distribution, a refined estimator can be developed and demonstrated to be closer to the ideal in comparison to the two and four data schemes, particularly in the context of CMB data with complex features such as diffuse foregrounds and point sources. The relative merits of the two and four data schemes are further evaluated by examining their performance under representative signal to noise ratios, with the results suggesting that the refined estimator outperforms both alternatives in the absence of precise sky modeling. When considering errors in modeling the sky signal, the performance of the refined estimator degrades relative to the two and four data schemes, with the differences in performance most pronounced at high signal to noise ratios, where the absence of exact sky modeling assumptions leads to banding effects that degrade the map quality. Ultimately, the relative effectiveness of the different estimators is dependent on a variety of factors, including their respective computational efficiencies, as better map quality does little good if the increased computing time proves prohibitive. To address this limitation, the computational requirements of the different estimators are compared, revealing that the two and four data schemes are significantly faster than the refined estimator, primarily due to the added overhead of incorporating additional constraints related to the noise distribution. Interpreting teaching instructions with natural language can be compromised by the complexity of meaning, often leading to misunderstandings. Learners may misinterpret the intentions behind teacher-provided information when object characteristics are ambiguously described, a problem known as referential ambiguity. We explore how principles from educational research, such as structure teaching and self-play, can alleviate this issue. Our study examines the effectiveness of self-play in reducing referential ambiguity and compares it to a structured approach where learners receive complementary information about the objects in question. Our findings suggest that self-play significantly outperforms structural approaches and that including additional hints does not necessarily improve learning outcomes in this context, but rather that self-play allows the learner to successfully infer the teacher's intentions in cases where the teacher provided an ambiguous description. Furthermore, experiments where the teacher did not provide object characteristics show that self-play still yields better results than a scenario where the learner relies solely on its prior knowledge. Our analysis provides new insights into the learning from instruction process and how self-play can help learners overcome referential ambiguity while also promoting generalization of learned knowledge. Our studies also reveal that instructions should ideally be encoded in a format that encourages self-play to help address referential ambiguity in real-world communication between teacher and learner.} Our findings confirm that self-play through reinforcement learning is a highly effective approach to addressing referential ambiguity and helps the learner to successfully interpret complex teacher-provided information. Our analysis for future work suggests that self-play will be an extremely valuable tool for teaching agents that learn through observation and imitation. Our additional experiments also show that self-play can help in situations where the teacher-provided description affects object interactions and control actions, further underscoring its utility as a versatile educational principle. Our studies do however reveal that self-play may not be an effective solution to mitigate another problem, known as semantic ambiguity, suggesting the necessity of distinct solutions to tackle different forms of communication failures. Our work further investigates the implications of assuming that teachers intentionally provide unambiguous object descriptions in various domains and observes that indeed in many educational contexts, teachers provide object characteristics that directly lead to successful learner outcomes in self-play scenarios. The advent of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) holds great potential for transforming communications systems. By harnessing their adaptability and swift deployment capabilities, it becomes feasible to supply content in densely populated areas or regions lacking essential infrastructure. In this study, we explore a UAV model that serves a maximum number of users at various locations within a set time frame. To achieve optimal trajectory planning, we develop a mixed-integer linear program for determining UAV arrival times, routes, and arrival times. Initially, we establish the minimum required arrival times for maximizing serving areas. Subsequently, we introduce a heuristic approach grounded in evolutionary algorithms to tackle the full problem, leveraging established trajectory plans as a starting point for generating efficient solutions. Experimental findings demonstrate that our proposed heuristic strategy outperforms a random exploration strategy while ensuring that all trajectory decisions can be effectively utilized. Furthermore, our model's scalability is thoroughly evaluated. In a real-world scenario, we utilize geographical data from Houston, Texas, and New York City to determine the UAV's serving capacity based on the model's optimized settings. Experimental results reveal that a single UAV can accommodate and satisfy the demands of nearly all users within a 10km radial radius in Houston and a 5km radial radius in New York City. A web-based interface has been created for visualizing the optimal trajectory plans for different cities. The link can be accessed at: http://korea.utang.org/index.html. A UTang repository containing the UTang package is available at https://github.com/tang-uni/UTang for sharing the implemented code to provide optimal solutions to the problem. In cases of limited computational resources, the UTang package can be leveraged to yield near-optimal solutions. A computational analysis indicates that a single core on a Intel Core i9 processor 16-Core 2.60GHz machine takes 11.6 seconds to yield an optimal solution, whereas a multi-core on the same machine takes 1.9 seconds to yield a near-optimal solution. A graph showing the UAV's free and occupied serving areas along with the optimized trajectory has been created through an integration of Google Maps API, Google Geocoding API, and D3.js, and can be accessed at: http://korea.utang.org/. The evolution of a single excitation has greater tolerance than its fermionic counterpart when dealing with circuit depth constraints. Conversely, the cost in terms of circuit depth for achieving a specified target value through qubit-excitation evolution is less unpredictable and results in more consistent costs compared to IBM's latest qubit models. Furthermore, these evolution types can concurrently perform different tasks, allowing the implementation of a quantum CTA program to accomplish two calculations at once, thereby enhancing efficiency and making the qubit-excitation evolution more suitable for cloud-based noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers, especially when dealing with deeper circuits. Among these models, the variational autoencoder and the deep generative decoder are prominent examples, simplifying the challenge of inferring rich representations from complex data. Typically, these models are trained using batch optimization techniques that are known to be inefficient. In this paper, a complementary approach involving online (stochastic gradient descent) and batch (batch gradient descent) training for the deep generative decoder is presented. The results indicate that online training leads to faster convergence and better results than batch training, and the achieved representations are comparable to those derived from variational autoencoders. The underlying reasons for these outcomes are explained by characterizing the learning objectives of online and batch training in terms of two different forms of mean squared error. The proposed approach is demonstrated to effectively reduce the liability associated with high-dimensional medical images.
