When conducting software maintenance, developers typically receive numerous requests for change, typically composed in natural language, to identify changes required. Unfortunately, there exist many requests issued by diverse individuals using varied language, leading to a complex task of identifying relevant changes. In recent years, researchers have made headway in processing this complex task through the application of natural language processing and machine-learning techniques. Despite these advancements, studies have significantly underrepresented the reviews provided in the Spanish language, highlighting a knowledge gap in this area. In an effort to address this gap, we conduct a meta-analysis combining three studies related to SPARQL query recommendation, leveraging a total of nine datasets, to understand the features extracted and performance achieved in this specific task and to compare outcomes across various machine-learning techniques and features. Moreover, we conduct an in-depth analysis of three particular studies, examining their respective results and implementing recommendations for future research. Ultimately, we discuss our findings and offer suggestions for future research in this area. This research paper explores the validity of the Collatz conjecture for a certain set of odd sequences with an infinite number of elements, which is then generalized to encompass all positive odd integers. By applying the principles of the greatest odd integer function and iterative processes, we demonstrate the conjecture's truth for all odd numbers. Similarly, we apply a minimizing function and traditional mathematical techniques to prove the conjecture for even numbers of the form 4k, thereby confirming the conjecture for all natural numbers. Additionally, we derive new minimizing and maximizing functions for certain functions associated with the conjecture, which in turn enables us to confirm the conjecture for all numbers. We also propose an alternative formulation of the conjecture known as the 'Elder Problem', which is comprised of the following two conditions: a number can be reached from another through a series of Collatz operations, and conversely, any number can be transformed into another only by applying Collatz operations. By employing our minimizing and maximizing functions, we validate this revised Elder Problem. Lastly, we validate four distinct generalized versions of the 'Elder Problem' by employing the same minimizing and maximizing functions. To guarantee that the next proposed match does not be rejected, two single-minded mechanism designs pre-specify a stable matching algorithm to apply in the case of receipt of the first bid. One such mechanism sets the optimal allocation according to bid estimates while another takes into account budget uncertainties in the allocation process. In contrast to prior approaches that address budget uncertainties, our novel mechanism, introduced as the ShortList Mechanism, relies on bidders providing merely their top choices of items, achievable by imposing an artificial limitation on those choices. A critical insight enables us to prove that the ShortList Mechanism yields essentially the same outcomes as an ideal mechanism that has complete knowledge of budget uncertainties, although the latter's complexity necessitates a custom-designed algorithm. Furthermore, the two mechanisms differ in their revenue only by a margin of at most a factor of four. Additionally, the ShortList Mechanism can be easily expanded to handle a scenario with multiple units of each item. In practice, its per-bidder computation complexity is comparable to other approaches, while its per-auction complexity scales better by a factor of the number of bidders and items. Theoretical evaluations confirm that the ShortList Mechanism's performance is superior to other determinate mechanisms in most cases, except in a specific scenario with binary budgets, it yields roughly a four-fold increase in revenue, whereas other approaches only achieve approximately 1.5 times the desired outcome. To demonstrate its practical applicability, our experiments show that the ShortList Mechanism successfully simulates the more reliable but inherently more complex mechanisms in various auction scenarios. A simple, self-contained online coding challenge is also presented to substantiate the theoretical findings by revealing its practical superiority. Current evaluation metrics for summarization models are inadequate, as they are based on labeled data and cannot guarantee high-quality summaries. To address this limitation, we propose a novel evaluation metric called SummScore, which can calculate scores automatically without human intervention. SummScore assesses summary quality across four dimensions: idea retrieval, sentence fluency, coherence, and length. Experimental findings indicate that SummScore outperforms existing metrics in evaluating four distinct copa genere models as well as a transformer-language model on ROBUST00 dataset. Moreover, SummScore successfully identifies high-quality summaries for specific topics and surpasses the performance of a leading retrieval-based copa system without human annotation. Finally, our analysis reveals that SummScore can detect biases in training data, which is critical for evaluating summarization models. In particular, SummScore highlights the strong performance of the best model on COVID-related topics, despite not being specifically trained on these topics during inference. In contrast, SummScore detects biases for several other topics where the models perform poorly. These results demonstrate that SummScore is an effective tool for evaluating the performance of summarization models. The proposed evaluation metric is compatible with existing ones and offers several advantages, such as compatibility with existing evaluation metrics, making it a convenient tool for researchers and practitioners to diagnose issues with existing models. Importantly, SummScore can be used to evaluate conversational summarization models, which is an emerging direction in natural language processing. The SummScore metric can be accessed at this repository: https://github.com/microsoft/SummScore. In the future, we aim to extend the efficacy of SummScore further by exploring additional advances in deep learning techniques that can improve the evaluation of summarization models. In particular, one promising future development is the integration of SummScore with network embedding methods, such as node representation learning, to enhance its performance. Additionally, SummScore can be seen as a form of end-to-end unsupervised abstractive summarization, which is an important future development. Although the current version of SummScore is tailored to copa genere summary generation, it can be adapted to develop summary quality metrics for other genres as well. In fact, one notable application of SummScore is the evaluation of conversational summarization models, which is an emerging direction in natural language processing and one that we believe SummScore is particularly well-suited for. We are reassessing the significance of thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence and determining their relevance on a particular scale. As earlier research by Betchov predicted decades ago, this scale is equivalent to the Kolmogorov length, although it's still many orders of magnitude greater than the average free path. This finding suggests that the non-random, or deterministic, form of the Navier-Stokes equation is insufficient for modeling the turbulence dissipation range within its own range of validity. Instead, the random fluctuations must be considered, even at scales far from the dissipation range, in order to accurately describe the turbulence. A simplified model incorporating random fluctuations based on the Lorentz model from the early 20th century is also proposed and discussed. This model is structurally similar to the original, but reflects the three-dimensional characteristics of hydrodynamic turbulence as opposed to the one-dimensional setup of the Lorentz model. A striking consequence of incorporating these random fluctuations is that the deterministic Navier-Stokes equation undergoes chaotic regime switching, or "tosses" the equation, rendering its solution essentially unpredictable beyond a short, fixed time frame, regardless of initial conditions precision. This unpredictability arises due to a particular fluctuation intensity threshold, above which initial condition precision losses quickly accumulate as time progresses. Furthermore, the randomness below this threshold, far from being merely infrequently active, is actually constantly active at a fluctation rate equivalent to a few times the non-thermal dissipation rate of the turbulence. Consequently, any hope for precisely solving the deterministic Navier-Stokes equation, even for an extended extended extended time frame, is effectively extinguished. A notable exception does exist though - if fluctuations are removed from the system, the deterministic Navier-Stokes equation does remain stable and solvable over an infinitely extended time frame. Currently, there's no suitable approach to adapt these models for query expansion due to significant changes in word and sentence probability distributions. We present a novel solution, AdaspaRNGL, an unsupervised adaptation method for query expansion that analyzes and learns from extended queries. By employing a cutting-edge NMT model that produces attention-based queries, we've developed two effective strategies: reverse attention and local copy attention. We've also introduced an experimental setup to compare the performance of different approaches and evaluated our method using a comprehensive dataset of extended queries. The results reveal that our approach outperforms existing benchmarks, achieving remarkable results with the existing models we've used - we've seen an impressive 8.2-fold increase in average sentence BLEU scores for extended queries, whereas another method yielded a 4.3-fold improvement. Moreover, our technique surpasses even better state-of-the-art models in query compression and has the added benefit of facilitating query compression as well as query expansion. We've validated the efficacy of our approach through a user study, showing that 63.36% of users prefer the queries generated by our algorithm over those produced by existing models, yielding notable improvements of 21.05% and 15.67% over baseline models for query accuracy and compression, respectively. We've made our implementation available on GitHub at https://github.com/HDRS-GUR/adasparql. This finding has implications for the Nichols algebras associated with irreducible Yetter-Drinfeld modules over the classical Weyl groups $\mathbb W_{n}$, revealing that these algebras have infinite dimensions, with the exception of three distinct cases: the $(2, 2)$ twist of $\mathbb S_{4}$, the $3$-dimensional algebra associated with $(\mathbb S_{5})^{G_{5}}$, and the $(\mathbb S_{6})^{G_{5}}$ twist. Furthermore, for specific real forms of classical groups, the conjugacy classes can be of type D or E, leading to the determination of corresponding algebraic properties for corresponding Yetter-Drinfeld modules over these groups. This, in turn, presents implications for Lie group cohomology calculations based on the given classifications. By analyzing additional examples, a more general conjecture is proposed, stating that for any connected simple Lie group $G$, the conjugacy classes can be classified as type A or E, which is subsequently realized through the application of nilpotent orbits classification over adjoint groups. This, in turn, presents new challenges and opportunities in the context of twisted Lie group cohomology and Lie algebra cohomology. This, in turn, presents an alternative perspective on Conjecture 1.1 and sheds light on the phenomenon of "over-specialization" in the context of twisted structures. By employing a theoretical framework of weakly nonlinear interactions, the researchers derived a specific scaling model for the small-scale geostrophic turbulence, while a established theory of rotating wave turbulence provided the framework for the modeling of large-scale inertial waves.  This theoretical framework allowed for the development of a comprehensive theory that combined both geostrophic and inertial wave turbulence.  Ultimately, this theoretical framework provided a good account of the observed behavior seen in experimental simulations, offering new insights into the complex phenomenon of combined geostrophic/inertial wave turbulence in rotating systems.  This theoretical framework provides a promising starting point through the use of an underlying kinetic closure scheme to further study the behavior of the wave mode, enabling the exploration of specific applications such as the vertical shear of angular frequency in wave ducts, the absorption of wave energy at boundaries, and the potential for the formation of small-scale inertial stirred modes. Pre-trained language models, exemplified by GPT-3, have exhibited an unexpected propensity for zero-shot learning. Specifically, incorporating a tiny dataset leads to impressive performance in downstream tasks. The process of fine-tuning language models in this context is dubbed "meta-tuning." Notably, the best results are often achieved with minimal, randomly selected data. This study investigates the meta-tuning phenomenon, drawing on GPT-3 and smaller models like GPT-2 and GPT-3 variants. The researchers evaluated the efficacy of meta-tuning with varying amounts of data across eight datasets and discovered that the most effective approach involves using the least amount of information. The findings also reveal that the existing state-of-the-art models, trained using supervised learning methods, surpass the performance of meta-tuned models; however, meta-tuning significantly enhances the ability to adapt to new tasks with just a small dataset. Additionally, the study explored techniques to bolster meta-tuning, including using multi-stage training and incorporating natural language benchmarks to select prompts. The researchers discovered that the existing prompts, developed by the model's creators, are superior to other choices and provide the best results among current options. The research outcomes provide valuable insights for handling large, unstructured datasets and may facilitate the development of more adaptable language models in the future. The code and data used in this research are available at https://github.com/mickgao/meta-tuning. Meta-tuned models, developed using this research, have been deployed to the HerdDB dataset and can be accessed at https://database.mickgao.com/. The model's validity is confirmed through a systematic comparison with Boltzmann simulations for one-dimensional planar and spherical rarefied gas flows. Successful applications of the $\nu$-model have been made to a planar shock wave, a spherical shock wave, and its results are compared to experimental data, demonstrating notable agreement. Furthermore, the $\nu$-model has been used to model gas rarefied flow in a sphere and its predictions compared to Boltzmann simulations, resulting in a satisfactory level of accuracy for statistical moments. This model has been implemented in a comprehensive software platform and its potential as a cutting-edge simulation tool for rarefied gas flows is introduced. Voice assistant technology has significantly progressed over the past decade, with a major limitation remaining in understanding voice inputs. While this objective may seem unattainable, it is an essential step for voice assistants to refine their capabilities and deliver more sophisticated responses. In our study, we present the SemParse dataset, a groundbreaking resource containing over 400k annotated utterances divided into two parts: 200k for training and 150k for assessing performance. The data spans a diverse set of semantic categories, covering a broad range of cross-domain applications that power virtual assistants like Alexa and Google Assistant. We establish and visualize new evaluation metrics that assess various aspects of semantic parsing performance and provide baseline results for cross-domain parsing, showing that current benchmarks can fall short of ideal performance by up to 20 percentage points on certain tasks. We freely distribute the SemParse dataset, a comprehensive resource that will benefit the development of more advanced voice input systems. You can access it at https://github.com/microsoft/semparse. In addition, our study highlights several areas for potential enhancement in high-performance systems and suggests avenues for further research. The SemParse dataset bears a strong resemblance to actual user input seen in voice assistant logs, underlining its practical utility in enhancing real-world voice input systems. Designing effective state observers for nonlinear epidemic models presents significant challenges. This difficulty stems from the inherent nonlinearity of these systems, which often follows the law of mass action and results in large, locally-dependent Lipschitz constants, making conventional design criteria unsuitable. This paper introduces a new state observer that improves estimation capabilities for nonlinear systems, including epidemic models, by mitigating the influence of nonlinearity in the error dynamics. To establish the observer's performance, sufficient conditions for convergence are formulated in the form of algebraic Riccati inequalities and linear matrix inequalities. These conditions provide a framework for evaluating and optimizing the observer's design for accurate state estimation. Additionally, this paper showcases the proposed observer's capability to accurately reconstruct infection and recovery counts in a real-world epidemic model. Compared to existing approaches, the presented observer offers improved estimation accuracy and resilience when subjected to the same fabrication errors. Furthermore, the efficacy of the proposed observer is demonstrated using a typical Sixgence vaccine pre-sale event, outperforming other estimators in both accuracy and antinoise capabilities. These findings showcase the efficacy of the proposed observer, offering a valuable tool for data analysis in applications such as epidemiology, medicine, biology, chemistry, and pharmacology. Various implementations and extensions of this proposed observer are also explored in this study. These extensions include developing a nonlinear observer to estimate time-varying infection rates, designing a state feedback controller to track a desired infection rate trajectory, and implementing a smooth control law to track a desired infection rate with robust stability guarantees. Lastly, the proposed observer design framework in this study offers the potential for expansion to other applications, such as image and signal processing. Furthermore, the presented numerical examples illustrate the superior performance of the proposed observer, outclassing other estimators in various scenarios. These examples also highlight the significant influence of fabrication errors, common in practice, on the observer's performance and demonstrate the proposed design's capability to achieve precise state reconstruction in real-world nonlinear epidemic models. Moreover, the achieved results show the proposed observer to be robust against critical high-level errors and demonstrate its ability to operate smoothly during data loss events, utilizing available information to achieve accurate state reconstruction, and offering a viable solution for building robust estimators. Lastly, the proposed design's flexibility and generalizability are demonstrated through its extension to other applications, allowing it to be further explored and developed to address fundamental challenges in diverse fields. By employing a transformer-inspired model to aggregate these descriptors, our approach outperforms static models significantly, and outdoes many temporal models that have been proposed recently. Several optimistic assumptions prevalent in federated learning literature are often unachievable in real-world scenarios. To counter this, an asynchronous framework provides a more realistic setting for testing federated learning's reliability. This setup reflects varying amounts of non-IID data across participants as well as heterogeneous client engagement influenced by computational and battery limitations. Additionally, the framework accommodates delayed client-server communication. To alleviate the high communication overhead associated with asynchronous online federated learning (ASO-Fed), we employed partial data sharing, which minimizes participants' communication loads and makes participating in the learning process more manageable. Notably, we proved the proposed ASO-Fed model converges, supported by simulations showcasing that, in asynchronous environments, ASO-Fed can achieve convergence comparable to Online-FedSGD with tenfold less communication. This achievement is particularly significant as it establishes that online and asynchronous frameworks are not necessarily at odds with each other, thus facilitating a more flexible and practical participation in online and asynchronous federated learning. To improve the efficiency of thin-film silicon solar cells with limited light absorption, researchers propose a back reflector that inhibits unnecessary absorption in the substrate materials. By simulating and analyzing nanostructured electron beams in 2D and 3D, simulations revealed the potential of photonic crystal arrays (grating periods: $\lambda$/2.5 to $\lambda$, with λ denoting the operating wavelength) to enhance photon recollection. These photonic crystal structures outperformed conventional aluminum coatings. Notably, incorporating a 1D photonic crystal passivated silicon substrate (with graphene coating) significantly enhanced the cell's absorption rate, achieving an average reflection rate of 91% for wavelengths within the 1.1-1.6 μm range. Subsequent numerical simulations indicated that an embedded quantum dot structure within the active thin silicon layer could further boost the cell's absorption capabilities. Notably, the overall absorption rate of 92% was reached at the operating wavelength of $\lambda$=1.5 μm, indicating that thin-film silicon solar cells with the suggested back reflector exhibit enhanced absorption properties compared to standard metal coatings. Moreover, these photonic crystal structures display improved absorption capabilities that surpass previous research findings. Furthermore, among proposed enhancement structures, the suggested back reflector and active thin silicon layer combination yielded the highest short-circuit current density (SCD), estimated at 34.3 mA/cm^2, indicating its considerable potential in efficiently converting light into electrical energy through thin-film silicon solar cells with enhanced illumination capabilities. These findings were verified using the software tools Meep and Fermi-Pasari for simulated simulations. As such, the suggested design presents a promising alternative for improving the efficiency of thin-film silicon solar cells with the ultimate goal of achieving higher conversion rates and increasing device efficiency. Optimal design and testing of the proposed structure, along with experimental validation, could potentially achieve an efficiency gain of 66% compared to conventional metal coatings. Notably, the suggested design exhibits the potential to surpass the theoretical efficiency limit of 66% for thin-film silicon solar cells, thereby opening up a new pathway to develop high-efficiency thin-film devices. Further investigation into the proposed design, along with theoretical predictions, could significantly contribute to the advancement of high-efficiency thin-film technology. A future experimental assessment of the design's efficacy is currently underway. The results from our simulation model have shown that thin-film silicon solar cells with the suggested structure achieve an efficiency gain of 66% over conventional metal coatings

We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but their construction in higher dimensions poses a significant challenge. Our coverings can be translated into constructions of high dimensional expanders with specific characteristics, such as those derived from Coxeter groups or other sources. Additionally, we have discovered a connection between the coverings and coverings of topological spaces which allows us to provide a unified explanation for the known constructions of high dimensional expanders derived from combinatorial methods. Furthermore, our method enables us to construct and give an alternative explanation for the alpha-beta constructions of expander complexes by Matz and Samuels. Moreover, our coverings can be used to provide constructions of categorical expanders in a novel and independent manner. Please see our paper for further details. Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. Additionally, the analysis of isothermal magnetization revealed a unique 1/3 magnetization plateau, corresponding to an 'up-up-down' arrangement of the Gd3+ ions. A notable increase in magnetic entropy was also observed in the GdInO3 system, originating from the inherent magnetic frustration within this compound. A model incorporating a classical spin Hamiltonian was employed to develop the theoretical phase diagram, showing a ground state dominated by weak easy-axis anisotropy and closely resembling that of an equilateral triangular-lattice system. This theoretical framework may be a valuable reference point for the interpretation of future experiments utilizing NMR, ESR, or muon-spin relaxation spectroscopy. Furthermore, the findings reveal the GdInO3 system to be the first representative of frustrated antiferromenets among the entire family of rare-earth indium oxides. A broader review is suggested to assess the prevalence of magnetic frustration within the rare-earth indium oxides family.

The application of graph embedding for predicting links in complex networks has shown remarkable success, but most real-world networks are sparse, which are currently underserved by this field. We propose the Sparse Structural Network Embedding (SSNE) model, which creates a representation of network nodes suitable for predicting links in these types of sparse networks. Initially, our model converts the network's adjacency matrix into a Sum of Normalized H-order Adjacency Matrix (SNHAM) through a novel computation method based on the highest degree node in the network. We also developed an optimization algorithm for SSNE that uses the sparse matrix divide-and-conquer technique and is combined with Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). Experimental results demonstrate that SSNE achieves equivalent or superior performance compared to existing models, such as GraphSAGE and PinSAGE, on both synthetic and real-world sparse network datasets, especially when the node order is H. Additionally, our research shows that SSNE has an advantage over other link prediction models in terms of efficiency, since it can achieve accurate prediction results with a low embedding vector length of 3 to 7. Therefore, our SSNE model effectively addresses the sparse structural network embedding challenge, making it suitable for spars Subgraph Sampling (SGS) link prediction method. A low-cost water jet process is employed to achieve a 6mm deep silicon etch, overcoming depth limitations and enabling the creation of a deep atomic vapor cell. Although initial vapor cell designs had minimum feature dimensions of 1.5mm, a novel two-chamber arrangement was developed to remove this depth constraint. A silicon substrate is sandwiched between two fused quartz spacers, separating regions containing indium tin oxide electrodes and photoresist-coated inhibitory surfaces. Electrical fields are applied to drive the Saffman-Taylor instability, propelling liquid from the inlet to fill the second chamber. This innovative design enhances signal quality and significantly expands the accessible parameter space for microwave spectroscopy experiments. This technique has the potential to modify the surface properties of silicon, enabling further advancements in atomic vapor cell technology. Furthermore, the developed process can induce significant sub-surface damage in silicon, but a subsequent polishing step is essential for improving silicon's surface properties in future applications. Additionally, the technique can be utilized in various other materials, like gallium arsenide, in future endeavors. The water jet process represents an accessible and versatile method for manufacturing complex silicon structures, particularly essential for enabling a 6mm deep atomic vapor cell used in blackbody-interferometer microwave spectroscopy, a technique that is highly suitable for implementing in integrated photonics. The deep vapor cell enables the study of extremely thin atomic layers, typically less than 0.1mm in thickness, which facilitates the detection of highly suppressed spectral signals. This novel integrated photonics platform enhances signal quality by reducing background interference from electromagnetic fields and increasing the atomic polarization population. The improved signal-to-noise ratio results from the increased atomic density near the silicon substrate. This innovative integrated photonics platform offers vast applications, including the study and detection of thin atomic layers, polarization, spin-dependent interactions, and other fundamental quantum phenomena, as well as potential uses in quantum computing, atomic clocks, and highly precise spectroscopy experiments. The water jet process represents an essential technology for manufacturing these deep vapor cells and exploring the deep sub-wavelength behavior of silicon. Moreover, the developed technique can significantly reduce the minimum feature size to sub-10nm, a size typically occupied by a water molecule, which is essential for enabling the study of sub-photon scale electromagnetic fields on silicon. This novel integrated photonics platform serves as an advanced tool for studying the unique electromagnetic interactions with silicon at the deep sub-wavelength level. The breakthrough in water jet technology, a cost-effective method, can accelerate future advancements in this innovative integrated photonics platform

Preemptive wildfire detection is critical for minimizing ecological harm, property damage, and human loss. Recent advances in Deep Learning have the potential to significantly enhance wildfire detection if informed by comprehensive, up-to-date wildfire data. In this work, a DL-based system for identifying wildfires from satellite images is proposed, accompanied by a newly developed wildfire dataset. The dataset comprises a collection of active and historical wildfires from 2018 to 2020, featuring Geospatial Context Information obtained from 16 different satellite images. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the proposed system's effectiveness is presented, demonstrating that it achieves an impressive 96.69% accuracy, a false positive rate of 2.51%, and a false negative rate of 3.22%. The proposed system outperforms existing wildfire detection methods across various indices. Moreover, a comparative evaluation of different DL architectures reveals that the combination of UNet and TransUNet architectures yields superior performance. Consequently, the proposed system is suitable for integrating with existing automated wildfire systems to improve their efficiency. The proposed dataset and system are publicly available at https://github.com/rguerrero12/AutoWorldFire. Key contributions of this research include a newly developed TransUNet architecture tailored for wildfire detection and an analytical framework for evaluating DL-based wildfire detection systems. Early detection and treatment of depression is essential to prevent severe consequences, making the use of machine learning and deep learning crucial for classifying depressive symptoms based on clinical data. However, acquiring labeled data in a clinical setting is challenging and often expensive, leading to the need for innovative data creation methods. One effective approach is to utilize publicly available social media posts to train models, providing them with data. A recently developed dataset, 'Mental Health Dataset', consists of 10,000 Instagram posts, each labeled as non-depression or one of three levels of depression, allowing researchers to classify mild, moderate, and severe stages of depression. The dataset was created through crowdsourcing by utilizing human annotators who applied established rules to label the posts. A description of the dataset, complete with explanation of its creation methodology, is provided in this paper. Additionally, the paper includes an evaluation benchmark, consisting of experiments performed using various baseline models, such as BERT, RoBERTa, LSTM, TF-IDF, and SVM, all of which achieved an accuracy of about 80% when classifying depression into its mild, moderate, and severe stages. The dataset is now available for further research at www.mentalhealthsemantics.org. A related paper, containing detailed explanation and results, can be accessed at the CVCUH-CST website. A study on stick-slip dynamics and the convergence of motion paths in systems governed by Coulomb friction is conducted. This robust design is enabled by leveraging Bass' algorithm to compute stabilizing controller gains through distributed solutions to Lyapunov equations. Specifically, each agent uses its own output weight matrix to compute a local controller, and global stability is guaranteed when all output weight matrices are consistent across the network. The escalating demand for bigger cooling systems to support increasingly larger numbers of cryogenic qubits in quantum computing applications is prompting innovation.
Through the National Quantum Initiative and Department of Energy's support, our work at the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center aims to create a 2-story, 12-story-tall cryogenic facility that uses a novel cryogenic architecture.
Featuring an innovative 'cool-down' design and a mix of cooling methods (4He/He-3 dual-stage, adiabatic cryogens, and steady-state cryogen refilling), the building minimizes energy consumption and reduces waste heat load per unit area compared to past facilities.
Combining cutting-edge superconducting materials and cutting-edge design principles for heat transfer and strength, the interior cryogenic equipment enables reliable, low-temperature operation across its entire volume.
In addition to its technical capabilities, the proposed facility also showcases sustainable energy efficiency and sustainability.

This paper presents an effective approach for locating fixed three-dimensional objects within large-scale metropolitan landscapes using an aggregation strategy for substantial amounts of two-dimensional image data, yielding significantly enhanced precision and robustness. A decentralized decision-making framework forms the foundation of this method, facilitating its capacity to handle large-scale data sets in a distributed and parallel manner. Evaluating this method with extensive image collections, encompassing nearly 400,000 images across 40 square kilometers of New York City and San Francisco, demonstrates its capacity to accurately reconstruct three-dimensional coordinates of objects, such as streetlights. Furthermore, the approach is shown to progressively improve in performance over time as the amount of collected data increases. Comparative tests against current top approaches demonstrate that this technique surpasses others in both precision and robustness. Comprehensive experimentation, encompassing trials under various challenging conditions, including diverse viewing angles, image resolution, distortion, time, and object association errors, showcases the effectiveness of this method, even when the input data is suboptimal. Moreover, the authors demonstrate that this simple yet powerful technique can be applied to locate temporary objects as well, such as those utilized in street signs for Groupon and Airbnb promotions. Moreover, the approach can be utilized for object classification by determining the likelihood of an object belonging to a particular category based on its observed position. This technique holds considerable potential for locating objects in unobserved metropolitan areas, thereby opening avenues for collecting more accurate metadata during object classification. We address the challenge of deconvolving sparse signals within seismic reflection inversion to retrieve the subsurface reflection coefficients with high resolution. Our model uses a synthesis-based sparse method involving both convex and non-convex regularization terms to yield l0 pseudo-norm approximations. This leads to an iterative algorithm utilizing proximal averaging that can be reformatted as a trainable neural network, optimizing through data-driven training. Our effectiveness is proven through numerical evaluations using synthetic data from 1-D seismic traces and 2-D wedge models in comparison to established techniques. Furthermore, we provide additional validation with a simulated Marmousi2 model and real-world data from a mid-continent salt dome. Our research shows that this new approach has the ability to retrieve attenuation, attenuation compensation, and reveals previously obscured details within seismic data, specifically in areas with complex structures such as salt domes. Our code is made available publicly for reproduction and future use. This research contributes a new, unique approach to seismic reflection inversion by leveraging deep learning technology. Our findings indicate that while there are limitations to recovering certain types of attenuation in cases of severe subsurface structure degradation, our proposed technique still achieves superior results in comparison to established methods. This research further highlights the effectiveness of our approach in uncovering previously inaccessible information within low-resolution seismic data by leveraging synthetic data in a data-driven setting. Our results demonstrate that our model can successfully extract reflection coefficients at multiple frequencies with an exceptionally high level of accuracy, specifically within the range of 5 to 15 Hz for the 2-D wedge models and simulated Marmousi2 model with a high R-square value of 0.9971. Our deep learning-based framework for sparse signal deconvolution successfully yields minimal error in comparison to the original input frequencies (0.9994, 0.9994, and 0.9996 for 5, 10, and 15 Hz, respectively) indicating its efficacy in retrieving deep subsurface reflection coefficients at various frequencies. This research further showcases the ability of our model to generalize and effectively extract reflection coefficients at an unseen frequency of 12 Hz in the presence of severe salt dome deformation, specifically in cases of sharp and gentle slopes. Our results demonstrate the ability of our model to significantly improve low-resolution seismic data by 44% in comparison to established methods. Understanding universal properties of a critical quantum spin chain model requires identifying key components of conformal field theory, notably the coefficients of operator product expansion, which describe operator fusion. Research suggests that these coefficients can be computed using wavefunction overlaps of low-energy states in the spin chain. We have demonstrated that central charge, conformal dimensions, and operator product expansion coefficients are encoded in wavefunction overlaps, accompanied by universal corrections that rely on cyclic orbifold CFT content. This approach provides a practical method for calculating crucial CFT parameters, ultimately enabling the identification of critical quantum spin chain models, like the one involving the O(N) symmetric Hamiltonian for N = 1, 2, 3. Moreover, for the specific case of N = 4, we have found that a particular two-loop anomaly contributes to the central charge, whereas analogous computations at the three-loop level reveal a non-zero result that requires a custom-made four-loop expansion. These findings have led to the discovery that a particular trigonometric identity is essential for ensuring that the recursion relation used to compute the central charge, and more broadly CFT parameters, remains consistent at all loop orders. This identity is derived from the fact that both the central charge and required two-loop contributions are constant and, as such, do not change at higher loop orders. Moreover, we have established the necessity of cusps in producing a consistent CFT limit for interactions between adjacent spins in the spin chain. These findings are also applicable to related systems, like those involving the O(N) symmetric Hamiltonian for values of N greater than 3. Moreover, we have discovered that both the central charge and essential two-loop anomaly contribute to conformal dimensions, while representing wavefunction overlaps in a specific manner allows for a straightforward method for computing these dimensions. Moreover, we have found the general form of leading universal corrections to wavefunction overlaps, which notably includes a term consisting of a product of conformal dimensions raised to the power of two. This research further sheds light on the specific form of leading universal corrections to conformal dimensions by revealing that they can be represented as the sum of Schrodinger-Coulomb gas formalism results, which consists of a series involving the convolution of Bessel K functions, amplified by conformal dimension-based exponential corrections, along with a term consisting of a product of conformal dimension squared, and as such, can potentially be computed at higher loop orders without any obstacles. Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed through machine learning. Although the problem is largely solved for contemporary languages, historical corpora pose significant challenges, primarily due to limited native speaker interaction and a lack of training data. Compounding this issue, historical texts lack standardized sentence structures and orthographies, making automated POS tagging more complex and error-prone. In light of these complexities, instead of assigning single tags with uncertainty, POS tagging algorithms should allow for probabilistic outcomes. We propose applying the concept of set-valued prediction, enabling POS taggers to suggest a set of potential tags rather than guessing a single one. The objective is to strike a balance between ensuring a high likelihood of the correct tag being included while minimizing the number of suggested candidates. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating set-valued prediction into existing state-of-the-art POS tagging algorithms yields more accurate and resilient results, particularly when encountering words not present in training datasets. The proposed technique is thus recommended for annotating historical language POS tags. The proposed approach is exemplified using the 17th and 18th century English datasets from the UAM Corpus. The research suggests that automating POS tags for these periods is a feasible task, although Standard English and Mid17th century English display distinct characteristics in their orthography, sentence structure, and vocabulary. In light of these differences, we contend that treating POS tagging as a binary classification task between classes representing formal and informal usage yields an accuracy enhancement of approximately 3.5%. The proposed approach is generally applicable to automated POS tagging in contemporary languages but exhibits relative effectiveness in datasets with standardized sentence structures and orthographies. As smart cities expand, they generate an increased need for automated conversion of human-specified demands into precise, machine-readable specifications. Nevertheless, human requirements often lack essential information, or they contain inaccuracies or ambiguities stemming from written English text. We introduce CitySpec, an innovative AI-powered system for formalizing smart city needs, which effectively bridges language gaps and resolves common data inconsistencies. The purpose of this research is to explain CitySpec's functionality by formalizing various urban needs, such as data from proposed projects on the City of Vancouver's website and citizen suggestions on the Talk Vancouver platform. These standardized specifications can then be executed using automated testing tools to assess the compatibility of city services with specified standards. The execution outcomes demonstrate that the formalized specifications can function as valid SQL queries within the city's database system. Furthermore, we analyze the benefits and limitations of using formalization in automated query generation, highlighting potential applications and potential partnerships for future collaborations between cities and research institutions. Our research presents an innovative technique that leverages hidden inverse utilities to counteract systematic errors in quantum gates. This method can incorporate existing corrections and synergize with other noise-reduction strategies like dynamical decoupling. By utilizing inverse utilities, the necessary gate distances are minimized and the number of necessary gates is optimized in controlled-N gate compositions. This advancement facilitates more efficient usage of quantum hardware, enabling the execution of intricate circuits like variational quantum eigensolvers, where numerous gates are required, to realize, for example, a hydrogen molecule, in which controlled-N gate compositions constitute a pivotal component. This method enhances circuit fidelity by reducing the impact of systematic errors without necessitating costly noise measurements. Additionally, the utilization of inverse utilities introduces a novel resource that can be utilized for error mitigation through machine learning techniques. To achieve this, we employed an adapted version of the Nallapara-Ramchandran algorithm and a neural network that forecasts utility values based on the density matrix of a quantum state. By applying this method to a specific implementation of a variational quantum eigensolver, where no additional qubits are employed, the fidelity of the solver has been enhanced, resulting in agreements with numerical solutions roughly three times more frequent than those utilizing the standard technique for computing ground-state energies of a molecule. The application of machine learning in image diagnostics within pathology and radiology is undergoing significant transformation.  Despite research-based promising outcomes with ML models, there is an underlying barrier to integrating these into clinical practices due to issues of interoperability.  The DICOM standard provides specifications for the representation, storage, and exchange of digital images and related information but the standard's complexity poses an obstacle to adoption in the ML field.  Therefore, there is a need for simplified data exchange protocols that enable seamless communication between ML systems and medical imaging devices, facilitating zero-shot learning and the learning by example capabilities.  In this paper, we demonstrate that eliminating the need for data preparation and annotation can achieve these learning capabilities through the use of simplified data exchange protocols, the specification of image processing pipelines, and the inclusion of metadata descriptions.  This protocol enables the direct training of ML models on datasets in various formats without needing to convert them into a standard format.  The protocol's effectiveness is validated by training a ML model for detecting chest abnormalities solely based on image file headers without any need for image data.  The discovery that experienced radiologists can make similar diagnoses by browsing random image file headers without needing to load them into a diagnostic platform is also a surprising outcome of this research.  The protocol and associated open-source implementation, along with the results of this study, are accessible at the following GitHub location, https://github.com/ado210-scale-free-ml/dicom-ml.  This research is an important step towards achieving scale-free ML, where the size of image collections no longer impact the effectiveness of ML models.  The outcome of this study further indicates that digital images are essentially static objects that do not require substantial computational resources to process, a fact often overlooked due to reliance on large-scale image classification as an entry point for ML research.  This research is an important contribution to the field of ML and aims to change the common perception that static objects have substantial computational requirements.  Furthermore, the outcome of this study challenges the prevailing notion that successful communication among devices necessarily incurs substantial network transfer costs.  A interesting consequence of this study is that static objects, such as images, can be efficiently communicated and processed through incremental byte-by-byte analysis, whereas transferring complete data objects may incur considerable redundancy during transfer, a fact revealed by comparative analysis of DICOM image transfers over various networks.  This research illustrates the efficacy of scale-free ML in image diagnostics and highlights its potential for widespread deployment in clinical and real-world settings due to its independence from substantial computational resources or data collections. We introduce an innovative neural architecture, dubbed DNA encoder (DNAEN), which can learn a compact, fixed-dimensional representation of DNA sequences in an unsupervised manner. DNAEN employs an innovative hierarchical encoder that comprises hierarchical multidimensional LSTM layers where the first layer processes DNA sequences in their native form and the second layer processes the output of the first layer as input, yielding a reduced representation of the original, lengthy sequence. We evaluated DNAEN's performance using a DNA classification dataset and compared it with existing reduced-dimensional latent representations. The results indicate that DNAEN successfully extracts reduced DNA representations of varying lengths, and these are comparable to the existing approaches in terms of classification performance, with the added benefit of being memory-efficient. We outline both an algebraic and a geometric approach to this method, with the latter presented here for the first time. Moreover, we discovered an additional momentum map, resulting in a dual pair of momentum maps, which under specific conditions can represent the process of Lie-Poisson systems collectivization. Consequently, applying symplectic Runge-Kutta methods to solve the system in its canonical form leads to integrators preserving coadjoint orbits and Casimirs precisely. We investigate the conservation of coadjoint orbits under the Runge-Kutta integrator by establishing an upper limit on its error magnitude. We further evaluate the accuracy of the method through two case studies. This new approach remains to be investigated further. Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel module called Orientation Convolution Network (OCN) that can be integrated into DCNNs to enhance their performance across various orientation scenarios. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of OCN in improving both classification accuracy and generality, especially in images with complex orientation disorders. Moreover, the experimental results show that the combined model achieves equivalent performance to state-of-the-art image recognition systems while operating at a significantly lower computational cost. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ziplab/OCNModule. This study highlights the potential of incorporating the OCN module into DCNNs to attain superior image recognition performance and enhanced generalizability across different orientation conditions. Additionally, the OCN module can be applied to various vision tasks, such as object detection and segmentation. Our research suggests that the conventional image-bias correction method can be substituted with end-to-end deep learning techniques like OCN to achieve more consistent performance across different datasets. Furthermore, the OCN module may also be employed as a regularization method to prevent overfitting in image classification tasks. Our study presents the potential benefits of combining OCN with other algorithms in various applications. Our study further indicates that the OCN module may also contribute to the expansion of the training dataset through image augmentation, thus facilitating the development of more unbiased models. Our research proposes a novel framework called Contrastive Contrastive Learning (C$^2$L) for semi-supervised learning, where the C$^2$L framework leverages the OCN module to learn discriminative features and has been shown to outperform other baselines in semi-supervised learning methods in our experiments. Our study demonstrates the potential applications of the OCN module in learning disentangled factors of images and investigating its application in semi-supervised learning in the future. Our research further proposes that the OCN module can be used as an efficient tool for de-identifying images in the future. Our study concludes that the OCN module has the potential to address several real-world issues, and suggests that the use of deep learning-based methods like OCN can lead to more consistent performance across different datasets. Our research provides a novel contribution to the regularization of image classification tasks and can be explored as an open research question in the future. Our study concludes the discussion on the potential benefits of the OCN module in various image processing applications.

Our method adheres to heavy quark symmetry constraints, allowing us to decompose and gradually remove the effects of lighter massive quarks as well as the intervening momentum regions, all while accurately controlling high-order asymptotic behavior. By employing this method, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of massive flavor contributions, calculate fourth-order quark mass corrections with a precise cutoff independence, and derive how pole mass renormalization group evolution relates to jet function evolution equations. Currently, the global pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 is being monitored using artificial intelligence systems that help identify lung infections in patients who have undergone computed tomography scans. Due to the risks associated with COVID-19, healthcare professionals are advised to prioritize using lower-dose scans, if possible. Our research focuses on determining whether machine learning models can effectively distinguish between COVID-19, lung infections caused by other illnesses (including pneumonia), and healthy individuals using lower-dose scans, which typically have lower image quality. By achieving this, it's possible to deploy AI systems that can help reduce the spread of the pandemic while minimizing the potential for data loss and measurement errors associated with low-dose Computed Tomography (CT) scans. Our research involves conducting a comprehensive test of several machine learning models, including support vector machines, logistic regression, and deep learning systems, to validate our approach. Additionally, the research demonstrates that the chosen method is robust to variations in scan dose and other external factors, which could simplify the deployment of the system in real-world applications. Furthermore, a method is briefly discussed for computing black hole metrics across multiple spatial dimensions. Our primary purpose in this text is to outline the analytical foundation necessary for developing a fully analytical and computable version of the Melvin universe model. This involves examining two-dimensional Melvin space-time, accompanied by a conceptual discussion of its physical characteristics. Additionally, an attempt is made to express the Melvin metric in terms of conformal coordinates. Conceptually reinterpreting the Melvin universe model leads to a description of its topology, along with an assessment of its potential as a spacetime model. Conceptually reinterpreting the Melvin space-time model yields a description of its horizon as extending infinitely, along with an understanding that, despite its name, it does not represent a boundary separating the interior from the exterior spatial realms. This unique characteristic arises due to a defunct concept that has been eliminated from modern quantum physics, reviving interest in earlier models like Melvin and Bonnor. Nonetheless, the interior Schwarzschild region remains genuinely confined within the broader exterior spatial realm. This distinction highlights a further peculiarity inherent to the Melvin space-time model.

Language learning dictionaries can facilitate vocabulary acquisition by supplying 
word definitions, although conventional dictionaries may struggle with 
capturing word meanings, resulting in inadequate learning materials. We 
create a generative dictionary that allows users to query an model similar 
to a GPT-3, which can then generate definitions for new words based on context 
information, unlike traditional dictionaries. Furthermore, the model can also 
be trained to define images, extending its educational applications. We analyze 
the efficacy of the dictionary through user studies and discover that the 
generative dictionary enhances vocabulary learning compared to conventional 
dictionaries. Additionally, the model demonstrates useful properties such as 
neutral and unbiased definition generation and the ability to explain out-of- 
date and technical words. Lastly, the model can also define images, expanding 
its applications. We hope that the proposed dictionary will serve as a foundation 
for developing more advanced language learning resources. We are now sharing the 
dictionary with the public and inviting users to contribute definitions 
(https://generative-dictionary.github.io). We welcome further research to 
improve the model, aiming for a future where the generative dictionary serves 
as a common reference for both learners and experts.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on Gaussian distributions, this new method utilizes a hidden Markov model with a hazard rate function comprised of a combination of anchor durations and acoustic features from previous frames. As a result, this model can easily incorporate the syntactic and phonetic information from acoustic features, thereby supplementing the standard mean-based duration statistic. Empirical evaluations on the LibriSpeech-960h dataset demonstrate that this approach surpasses previously proposed anchor-based and neural distribution-based methods for speech synthesis duration accuracy. Moreover, we show that a simple modification to the HMM training procedure can significantly enhance the model's performance, leading to the best results achieved among all compared methods. Finally, the efficacy of this model is confirmed through objective and subjective evaluations, resulting in improved speech quality and correctness. The code for this model is available online at the repository https://github.com/DioMiao/HiMed. 

Even modest enhancements to this new model's performance lead to notable gains in the model's capacity to generalize. Notably, the model obtains a speech quality score of 0.65 and a correct word recognition rate of 91.95% on the LibriTTS dataset, outperforming the standard HMM-GMM system by 3.51% in the word recognition rate and 2.9% in the speech quality score. As a result, this model is deemed suitable for industrial applications that necessitate robustness to unseen test data. Moreover, the subjective evaluations reveal that the model achieves a mean opinion score (MOS) of 4.71, outperforming the HMM-GMM system by 0.43 in the MOS score. Furthermore, we found that even though this model can easily incorporate the standard mean-based duration statistic, it remains distinct from previously proposed neural distribution models that also utilize the standard mean-based duration statistic. Consequently, this model is deemed an enhancement to previously proposed neural distribution models that are primarily designed for speech synthesis but can now be leveraged to compute a more accurate standard mean-based duration statistic.

In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if, for any two vertices, a single set vertex is positioned at different distances from the two vertices. The problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, called the Metric Dimension problem, has been a subject of research since the 1970s. The problem was found to be NP-hard, with parameterization by the vertex cover number yielding fixed-parameter tractability. However, the complexity under different parameters remained unclear until our recent discovery, where the problem was found to be W[1]-hard when parameterized by the feedback vertex set number. Additionally, we found that parameterization by the vertex cover number results in the problem not admitting a polynomial kernel unless a significant assumption holds. While the problem remains open under the vertex cover number, we found fixed-parameter tractability when parameterizing the problem by distance to cluster or co-cluster. The results were achieved through the design of a new algorithm that uses the Contracting algorithm technique. Furthermore, we derived fixed-parameter tractability under parameterization by the neighborhood correlation number and established that the problem, when parameterized solely by the last parameter, belongs to the class XP. The study concludes with the observation that the problem, when parameterized by the distance to cluster or co-cluster, does not admit a polynomial kernel unless a significant assumption holds. The research reveals the complexity of the Metric Dimension problem under various parameterizations, paving the way for further research in the field. Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and their existence and structures are shown for any directed space.  Notably, these spaces have distinct structures compared to powerdomains of directed-complete partial orders with Scott topology and other previously-introduced powerspaces.  Relationships between these spaces and subspaces of directed spaces are investigated, and specific cases are studied for discrete spaces, metric spaces, and function spaces.  Finally, the paper discusses indexed powerspaces of directed spaces, and their applications in the study of directed functions and directed continuous functions.  This work identifies general properties of directed spaces and their powerdomains without relying on free algebraic constructions, as well as differences between directed spaces and dp-spaces - a type of quotient space - through the relationship of being finite-determined (fd) and being a directed space.  Powerdomains of fd spaces are also studied, and the paper identifies discrepancies between being directed and being fd, particularly in the context of discrete spaces.  The paper ultimately determines the distinctness of the powerdomain construction, powerdomain construction via d-powerspaces, and the powerdomain construction for directed spaces via the Mazur-Sierpinski double negation theorem.  The paper concludes by establishing the equivalence of different constructions for directed spaces, with the powerdomain construction being equivalent to the construction of the upper sublocale of the compactification of the one-point compactification of the directed space and its discrete extension.  The paper ends with a discussion on whether directed spaces can serve as a universal base for the study of powerdomains of dp-spaces and fd spaces.  The last part of the work specifically looks at the powerdomain of the discrete space in the context of general directed spaces, and identifies two subcases: the case where the powerdomain is a discrete space, and the case where the powerdomain is not a discrete space - in this latter case, the powerdomain of the discrete space is homeomorphic to the compactification of the one-point compactification of the discrete space.  The paper concludes that directed spaces possess sufficient universality to serve as a base for the study of powerdomains of discrete spaces, while the powerdomain construction of directed spaces is not exhaustive as it fails to yield powerdomains for other types of directed spaces,

This method avoids the need to explicitly state evaluation depths in termination proofs for base recursion patterns. This research paper introduces an advanced optical nanoantenna design, consisting of a hybrid silicon nanoring that achieves high directed light emission and enhanced light absorption, even at low input powers. The targeted structure is a compact, three-part nanoring created from air islands on top of a thin silicon substrate. Our study specifically examines a 220 nm diameter, 10 nm thickness silicon nanoring, embedded in a 50 nm thick medium. Our findings demonstrate that by incorporating a silicon substrate, the efficiency of light emission emission can increase up to 60%, far exceeding the maximum possible light emission efficiency of 40%, as established by and efficient dipole source. Additionally, the designed nanoantenna acts as an efficient Mie antenna, where an infrared wave interacts with the structure, resulting in a highly efficient scattering effect. Our analysis shows that under these conditions, the scattering wave overpowers the incident wave in proportion, indicating a robust active Mie scattering phenomenon. The developed nanoantenna layout possesses excellent scalability, which is essential for its adoption in future photonic devices. Furthermore, the device's functionality extends beyond directed light emission; it can also amplify light absorption by emitters trapped within its boundaries, achieving a maximum absorption enhancement of 230 times. Moreover, the design is versatile and adaptable for a variety of semiconductor materials with various colors of emission. The demonstrated directed light emission and enhanced light absorption provide two major advantages for future optoelectronic applications: the capability to produce coherent light from non-coherent sources and the ability to increase the efficiency of energy conversion from light energy into electrical energy. The developed device is also compatible with the electrostatic release of nanoparticles, which paves the way for its integration in a plasmonic-based sensor platform that detects circulating circulating DS-DNA. The conventional DNA detection method involves measuring a signal from a fluorescent marker attached to the complementary DNA strand after it hybridizes with the target DNA. However, it has been found that the conventional method fails to amplify the fluorescence signal. In contrast, the DNA used as the local source of light is not affected by the fluorescence and the DS-DNA is not damaged during hybridization. As a result, the design of the nanoantenna and the mechanism of the DNA-based active Mie scattering represent significant breakthroughs in the field of the research. The study offers new perspectives for the development of novel photonic devices that leverage DS-DNA-based active Mie scattering. In nuclear and particle physics, being able to measure the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, accessible through large TPCs with ionization signals, is vital for understanding dark matter phenomena, such as detecting WIMPs, and for analyzing neutrino directions, particularly in relation to their sources, like supernovae. However, this measurement is challenging with liquid scintillators because the scattering particles tend to deposit their energy in a non-proportional, highly collimated form resulting from the inelastic collisions and non-linear energy transfer, which makes it difficult to use time-of-flight measurements for determining directions. A novel reconstruction technique has been proposed, employing machine learning to establish a collimation of energy depositions, by representing these depositions in a 3D array and assigning each event a score based on whether it meets the required criteria. Demonstrating its effectiveness, this new technique was applied to events simulated from LUX-Zeplin and PTOLEMY dark matter experiments as well as to real scintillator data from the Porton Down Research Laboratory's Cherenkov time projection chamber. Utilizing datasets with ultraviolet light, gamma rays and cosmic muons, the technique was tested to assess its performance and evaluate false positive rates. By employing clustering and supervision with trained physics-based models, the technique achieves an accuracy of about 80% for determining direction in LUX-Zeplin and PTOLEMY's context, while achieving an accuracy of about 70% for understanding direction in the PDRCL's events. The technique has significant advantages over traditional methods because it's independent of physical assumptions and doesn't necessitate event reconstruction time. The technique has the capability of improving the sensitivity of LUX-Zeplin, PTOLEMY and similar detectors by at least one order of magnitude, in relation to directional recoil analysis. The technique has the potential of being adapted to other collimated particle searches. The technique's relevant source code has been made accessible through GitHub, with the necessary extensions for different projects being required. A physics-based model for particle reconstruction has been implemented as part of the code, allowing the technique to work effectively even with un-supervised datasets. A detailed explanation of the technique's underlying principles has been provided, illustrating its applicability to various collimated particle analysis projects. The technique can be utilized in context of particle reconstruction for any collimated particle analysis by demonstrating its effectiveness in LUX-Zeplin and PDRCL contexts and the potential for its extension to other projects. A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior is crucial for developing effective road safety solutions and policies. However, accurately predicting driver behavior is a significant challenge due to its complex association with various contextual and sequential factors. One promising approach for predicting behavior is behavior prediction using machine learning, particularly sequence-to-event regression. In this paper, we investigate commercial driving behavior and propose the application of two advanced deep learning models, based on contextual and sequential information, to predict incidents. These models utilize Bayesian Neural Networks, Bayesian Gaussian Processes, and incorporate context and sequence data, which we demonstrate are superior to existing Markov-based methods. Our results indicate a notable correlation between these predictions and actual incidents in certain contexts, such as weather and day of theweek. Additionally, our analysis reveals that predicted incidents occur more frequently on major roads and are more likely to involve rear-end collisions. Our findings suggest that incident predictions could serve as a cost-effective and efficient solution for real-time risk detection and incident prevention. In practical terms, our proposed methods have the potential to be integrated into intelligent driving systems and receive updates at a rapid pace via machine learning, thus enabling a range of potential applications, such as risk detection and incident prevention. As such, our proposed sequence-to-event regression framework has far-reaching implications for a broad range of predictive problems. These findings were further validated in a real-world work environment where they have been implemented in a traffic management system for reducing commuting times in Hong Kong. We used the 64-m Sardinia Radio Telescope to study the emission of nearby spiral galaxies in the K band. Our goal was to detect the Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) produced by spinning dust grains in the galaxies' dust, a signature first detected by COBE and supported by WMAP data. We conducted a 4-hour observation using the telescope's Large Millimetric Array (LMA) and analyzed the data from January 2011. The galaxies we observed were NGC 3627, NGC 4254, NGC 4736, and NGC 5055, chosen based on their distance, age, color, and luminosity. We employed two different data analysis approaches: a correlation-based search and a circular map search, but neither yielded a notable signal. Our analysis also included a cross-check of the data using ARKID, a software designed to detect millimetric and submillimetric radiation intensity variations. In the frequency range of 2 to 4 GHz, we did not observe any intensity variations above 20 mK, confirming that the detected intensities were consistent with the cosmic microwave background. Leveraging the telescope's capabilities and analyzing four nearby spiral galaxies did not enable us to detect the Anomalous Microwave Emission of dust. Our findings are based on the data collected and analyzed as part of the SPIREX campaign. The observed galaxies' radiowave emission was consistent with the existing literature, while ARKID-enabled us to conduct a novel spatial analysis of the radiowave intensity variations. The circular map search did not reveal any anomalies, although the lack of a notable signal from the LMA was considered due to its relatively small collecting area. The observed galaxies did not exhibit anomalous radiowave intensity variations, either. A future upgrade to the LMA, increasing its collecting area to five times the current value, should enhance the facility's capabilities and sensitivity. The analysis confirmed that the observed variations were consistent with the existing knowledge and did not point to the presence of AME; however, this absence of a signal does not rule out the possibility of a detectable Anomalous Microwave Emission in more powerful galaxy radio emissions. Consequently, a more thorough and systematic investigation of our galaxy and neighboring spiral galaxies is recommended to identify potential anomalies consistent with the existing research. The study further highlights the significance of the 64-m Sardinia Radio Telescope in analyzing radiowave intensity variations and suggests a greater use of the facility in the field. Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated nature belies a significant ferroelectric phase transition accompanied by an exceptionally large entropy variation and both electrocaloric and barocaloric properties. For decades, researchers have disputed the underlying cause of the significant entropy change, but this issue is now resolved using a comprehensive approach that incorporates density functional theory-based phonon calculations, inelastic neutron scattering, and additional neutron scattering experiments. In contrast to the previously assumed, albeit widely adopted model of entropy involving disorder across the high-symmetry phase's mirror plane, it is now clear that this simplistic model is invalid. Instead, it is discovered that the significant entropy originates from the low-frequency wobbling of ammonium ions in this phase, which produces small to negligible harmonic components. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for vibrational entropy stemming from broad energy minima, which may be just as significant as configurational entropy due to crystallographic disorder in discovering molecular materials with functional properties. Furthermore, they show that ammonium sulfate undergoes a typical temperature instability of the high-symmetry phase rather than transitioning into a low-symmetry phase with mirror plane symmetry broken, as some earlier experiments suggested. Finally, it is verified that this compound exhibits pronounced electrocaloric and barocaloric effects, which could be useful in electrorefrigeration.
