In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes opt for a less than optimal strategy known as probability-matching, which means choosing options based on their reward probabilities, as opposed to the optimal strategy, maximization, which involves always selecting the option with the highest reward.  Despite years of study, the factors that lead to probability-matching are still unclear and highly contested.  To address this, a team developed an innovative model of learning that is capable of both probability-matching and maximization through two distinct mechanisms of decision-making.  Utilizing this model, they investigated the effects of different emotional states, such as fear and pleasure, as well as social factors, like the presence of others, on decision-making.  Their analysis reveals that, under certain emotional and social conditions, probability-matching is the preferred choice, whereas maximization is preferred in more extreme situations.  This new model offers a unique approach to understanding the complexities of probabilistic learning and offers a promising framework for further exploration of the various factors that influence decision-making in both humans and animals.  Furthermore, it has the potential to be applied in fields such as neuroscience, cognitive psychology, and artificial intelligence.  A simple Python program has also been developed to simulate and assess the model's capabilities.  A detailed description of the program's functionality and ongoing work as well as potential future directions have also been provided.  Ultimately, the probability-matching phenomenon continues to fascinate both cognitive psychologists and AI researchers and this new model represents an important step forward in our efforts to comprehend the mechanisms that underlie decision-making in both animals and machines.  We encourage your feedback regarding the model's relevance to probability-matching and any suggestions you may have for further research. A simple interactive program has been developed using Python to simulate and assess the model's capabilities at http://cplexgym.net/pmmodel.py.  We are confident that this new model will aid in our ongoing efforts to comprehend the complexities of probabilistic learning and decision-making in both animals and machines. The continuous Fréchet distance c-approximate near neighbor problem involves precomputing a data structure that efficiently finds closest polygonal curves within a certain radius from query curves, considering an approximation factor for potential inaccuracies. This study primarily investigates this problem using time series curves, providing a comprehensive analysis for one-dimensional curves. By improving existing results, the research offers multiple tradeoffs between approximation quality, preprocessing efficiency, and query speed. Key outcomes include achieving the same performance as the optimal but with an increased preprocessing cost, and demonstrating that using a product data structure for two dimensions leads to significantly faster query times at the expense of more complex preprocessing. Additionally, lower bounds were established for both scenarios, showing that existing results are essentially optimal. Moreover, the research successfully tested its approaches using synthetic data, and related approaches for discrete curves were also explored, revealing some of the key challenges in that domain. Lastly, the study partially solved the problem for the case involving an infinite number of points in the curves, offering lower bounds as well as a probabilistic solution that approaches optimality. However, it remains unclear if this approach can be made deterministic. Further work would be necessary to address the case where the number of points is finite and reduce the dimensionality of the curve points, effectively making the problem more general and substantial. Therefore, the research identifies several promising avenues for future investigation. To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of existing mitigations lies in their inability to leverage measurements from subsequent rounds effectively. This paper develops a novel mitigation approach, referred to as round-integrated measurement error mitigation (RIM), which integrates noise impact across multiple rounds in a quantum circuit, thus enhancing performance in scenarios with deep or frequent measurement mechanisms. By combing high-performing optimizers with the influence of intervening measurements, RIM demonstrates substantial improvements, offering a valuable addition to the toolset for mitigating measurement errors. Experimental outcomes for both synthetic and real-world datasets are provided to demonstrate the efficacy of this new mitigations technique. Furthermore, we present a universal decomposition of a qubit's evolution under SPAM (systematic preparation and measurement) that can inform any mitigation strategy, offering increased flexibility and transference of knowledge across different algorithms and programs. This new decomposition contributes significantly to the mitigation field, as well as SPAM-unfolding research in general, and has the potential to be applied to the majority of gate sets that have a closed-form evolution representation, such as the Pauli basis. By utilizing this decomposition, we introduce a new mitigation strategy called gate-integrated measurement error mitigation (GIM). Comparative analysis reveals that both RIM and GIM result in superior noise reduction compared to existing mitigations, while equally enhancing the accuracy of model predictions. Remarkably, our findings indicate that integrating noise mitigation and model learning in a single step produces substantial gains in both tasks, thus warranting the development of novel learning algorithms that merge these two objectives. Moreover, our research shows that the round-integrated measurement error mitigation strategy is applicable to a wide range of real-world scenarios, such as combining NISQ and near-algorithmic tasks. Consequently, we suggest incorporating the round-integrated measurement integrated mitigation strategy into the execution of quantum circuits in order to further accelerate the advancement of NISQ devices. This novel integrated strategy for mitigating measurement errors may be executed via software modification at the quantum programming level, thus facilitating widespread adoption. Furthermore, our research offers a quantification of the trade-off between execution time and performance error, thus informing decisions regarding the optimal balance between execution efficiency and performance when selecting a mitigation strategy. By merging measurement error mitigation and model learning in the postprocessing stage, we propose a new framework for advancing NISQ device applications, thus pushing the boundaries of what is feasible with these devices. This study focuses on utilizing convention-based learning to teach humans about the robot's control methods. By identifying instances where the control interface's movements match the robot's motion, humans can learn the desired convention. Additionally, the robot can be programmed to include instructional movements when operating tools, making it easier for humans to comprehend the relationship between the control interface and the robot's motion. Our experiments show that the human operators' understanding of the robot's conventions is substantially enhanced when the robot incorporates instructional movements in conjunction with the identification phase. Research into two-dimensional arrays with optimized sparse patterns is gaining traction due to their numerous wireless communication applications. Studies on this topic are primarily centered around optimizing the arrangement of secondaries in a given area, resulting in unique geometric shapes. However, the requirements for array elements that can be placed anywhere are often non-geometric in nature, leading to a lack of understanding within the communication community. This work addresses this disparity by providing a mathematical framework along with concrete proposals that can tackle this more general challenge. Specifically, this framework is applied to the particular cases of controlling interference, shaping the far-field phase pattern, and enabling secure communication using a double-ring array, showcasing its effectiveness. These cases highlight the versatility of this framework and demonstrate its feasibility in tackling real-world problems. Furthermore, this work also explores the feasibility of implementing these arrays using existing technologies such as LED strips, enabling a closer look at their practical implications. Finally, this work exhibits the array elements positioned at viable locations in each proposal, serving as a starting point for further optimization if desired. Although this analysis is confined to 2D arrays, the developed framework is versatile and can be extended to more complex scenarios, such as 1D or three-dimensional arrays. Additionally, this work does not delve into frequency domain considerations, focusing instead on time-domain optimization, including simulations of the array's frequency-based phase delays. Ultimately, this work has the potential to pave the way for the widespread adoption of these arrays in various communication technologies. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional challenge. In functions-based object reconstructions, the distortions are represented by additional terms reflecting the non-linear relationship between pixel values and radiation intensity. This study aims to tackle these distortions by developing a non-linear regularization method for CT reconstruction. Our research indicates that the distortion effects can be reduced by employing two novel iterative algorithms featuring regularization that mimics low-frequency filtering. These proposed algorithms, supported by numerical simulations, demonstrate a capacity to counteract the distortion effects by introducing additional terms reflecting the non-linear relationship between pixel values and radiation intensity. Our research outcomes provide further insights into the potential ways to counteract the distortion effects through corrected low-frequency filtering or high-frequency enhancement. Our study's findings hold promising prospects for enhancing image quality in CT reconstructions. Our research can also be extended to other applications, including nuclear medicine, magnetic resonance imaging, radiotherapy, radio astronomy, astronomical and particle physics imaging, by incorporating attenuation factors unique to each modality. We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, these findings also indicate that both spillover effects and a correct description of the nonlocal electron behavior are essential for a thorough understanding of how light propagates through thin metallic areas. Furthermore, a quantum hydrodynamics model which also considers quantum pumped effects could potentially reveal inherent unidirectional electron circulation, which current studies fail to explain. Additionally, we demonstrate that a hydrodynamics model which uses a quantum description of nonlocal electron behavior outperforms one based on a classical description, particularly as the gap narrows. Finally, we verify that a quantum hydrodynamics model which also includes quantum pumped effects accurately reproduces the interference pattern produced by the propagation of light through a narrow gap and the resulting photoemission, which correlates with existing experimental findings. In conclusion, our paper shows that accurate models of light propagation through thin metallic areas, which also consider local spillover, nonlocal behavior, classical or quantum nature, and quantum pumped effects, generate pleasing results, which may be crucial for understanding various other phenomena. We recommend that such a model be applied to a quantum hydrodynamics description of nonlinear photoemission in order to gain insight into other high-intensity light-matter interactions. We anticipate that such a model will also contribute to an understanding of other related phenomena beyond the scope of this paper. Time-based data refers to information measured against the backdrop of time, giving it a distinct structural context that forms the foundation of its constituent parts. When dealing with multi-variable data sets that change over time, we anticipate observing interconnected patterns, long-term fluctuations, seasonal variations, and correlations across different variables. In contrast, longitudinal data often displays relationships between and within individual units over time, including both intra- and inter-subject correlations. While analyzing time series and longitudinal data differs in certain aspects, they frequently employ similar visual display methods. Our approach focuses on creating an interactive framework that allows users to explore and dissect the time-based components of these data types, including how to transform and manipulate the data. Given that temporal data often crosses paths with spatial data, our method also accounts for compiling data from geographic areas, though the focus remains on the temporal aspect. Our data science tools and methods are presented in the form of shading, a Python package that provides a unified framework for time-based data analysis. Our method also outlines a step-by-step data science pipeline that showcases shading's capabilities through its applications to two distinct datasets. Secondly, we used shading to create visualizations and insights from real data from bike and car sharing systems in the United States, including correlations between bike and car usage and how they are affected by weather. The promising potential of extracting valuable insights from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has emerged as a crucial area of study, as machine learning models can assist healthcare professionals in decision-making to enhance overall healthcare quality. Advances in sequential and graph-based machine learning architectures have enabled the development of more effective clinical models, showcasing their versatility. Even though GNNs have gained popularity for analyzing patient data, the present understanding of their capabilities and strengths in the context of EHR analysis remains limited. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a comprehensive literature review focusing on the use of GNNs for processing EHRs, the classification of models based on their temporal aspect, the evaluation of their performance, and the associated challenges and future research directions. Through our review of 122 relevant studies, we were able to distill essential insights and contributions, enabling us to outline key research avenues for the future. While certain topics like tabular vs. structured data, the use of graph representation for molecular data, and the understanding of GNNs' interpretability have become clear areas of focus, other areas like dealing with long/short sequences and structured data with varying degrees of granularity remain unexplored. Our review uncovered numerous articles evaluating the performance of GNNs relative to GDNNs and tabular methods, although only a small subset focused on tabular and structured data separately. From our analysis, we identified trends in recent publications indicating that GNNs generally outperform by slight margins in most tasks, but the use of tabular methods is often comparable to or even better than GNNs under certain circumstances. Our review shed light on the specific challenges of dealing with data structures, long/short sequences, and unstructured data with varying degrees of granularity, highlighting opportunities for future research in these areas. As a result of our study, we were able to outline distinct research avenues for the exploration of GNNs in the analysis of EHRs, aiming to guide future studies and contribute to our current understanding of the use of GNNs in this field. Our work also compares the concept of graph representation and the type of information it conveys in the analysis of EHRs with other medical domains, identifying similarities and differences. Our review includes examples of specific graph-based methods developed to address specific tasks and highlights the need for studies evaluating the understanding of GNNs' interpretability. Our study marks the first attempt at distill essential insights and contributions from 122 relevant studies, providing a concise overview of the use of GNNs in the analysis of EHR

Using a memory function formalism, the dynamical behavior of the dielectric response in ac electric fields is examined for nonpolarizable liquids containing charged molecules. Analytical expressions are derived for the dielectric spectrum, acoustic relaxation, and related opalescences, each applied to an electrolyte solution surrounding a spherical surface. It's observed that, close to this charged sphere, solvent polarization makes the electrostatic potential highly nonlinear and thereby considerably influences the dielectric behavior, particularly in low-frequency ranges, a phenomenon not predicted by linear theories. For a monovalent salt in close proximity to a model cation, simulations of dielectric relaxation display a pronounced departure from the expected Debye-Huckel behavior, a deviation that's most apparent at low frequencies and optimal salt concentrations around 0.01 M. A four-step memory function model, used to describe dielectric behavior, involves a successively decaying series of Lorentzian curves, each associated with increasing molecular sizes. Ultimately, this work aims to contribute to our understanding of the dielectric behavior observed in various optical studies of liquid electrolytes. We anticipate that, in the high-frequency region, this model will facilitate the identification of smaller solvation molecules that might otherwise remain undetected. Furthermore, it is hoped that this work, focused on dielectric relaxation, can provide a valuable framework for interpreting various optical phenomena. We are also able to provide dielectric data and fitting parameters for the EH2 water model in several relevant frequencies, extending the model's applicability to specific situations. A direct link between outage probability, energy consumption, and energy efficiency is established, followed by a formulation of the optimization problem to maximize energy efficiency under the constraint of achieving a target outage probability. A practical scheduling and power allocation strategy is then proposed to minimize power and maximize energy efficiency, characterized by the use of a main relay and residual diversity signals. Interestingly, the results demonstrate that network coding may not always improve energy efficiency, and in some instances may even decrease it compared to a benchmark without network coding. However, with a strict outage constraint, the proposed MDNC strategy is shown to surpass a conventional approach without network coding in terms of energy efficiency. Subjecting solid materials to an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a laboratory-based source causes significant changes in the material's electronic structure, resulting in high-energy ionization and electron removal. This, in turn, leads to changes in measured X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy (XANES) curves as the material absorbs more photons. High-energy ionization, nonlinear effects, and temporary changes to the material's electronic structure all contribute to fluence-dependent changes observed in non-linear XANES. To date, experiments have primarily studied nonlinear XANES in copper, carbon, and nitrogen, but exploring a range of elements, particularly those with lower ionization energies, could provide new insights into the impact of high-intensity X-rays on materials. For example, probing elements in insulating materials could uncover effects on valence band ionization potential, while investigating elements in metals could reveal the influence of their d-band filling on the XANES measurement. Moreover, variation of band filling among different metals could make their temporary changes to band edge position a visible occurrence. This could provide an exciting opportunity for leveraging high-intensity X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy to investigate the band edge modulation, previously observed in density functional theory, but previously elusive to measure. To facilitate further investigations, a detailed simulation has been developed to guide interpretation of non-linear XANES data and explore the impact of varying electron number, mass, and charge across different materials. This simulation has been validated through comparison to experimental and calculated data for copper, carbon, and nitrogen. Building on existing knowledge, it is position to fill a critical gap in the understanding of high-intensity X-ray matter interaction, particularly in the increasingly accessible intensity region of laboratory-based sources, and their applicability in XANES measurement. Moreover, it is an advancement towards leveraging high-intensity X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy to investigate the band edge modulation, a phenomenon that has shown to occur under high-intensity condition but was considered cannot be measured under moderate intensity condition. 

Key words: high-intensity X-ray, X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy, nonlinear effect, electronic structure modification, temporary change, inhomogeneous broadening, simulated absorption curve, band edge modulation, electron removal.

The application of a Deep Neural Network in Automatic Modulation Classification (AMC) exhibits enhanced performance compared to traditional methods even in harsh wireless environments, but this can be compromised by targeted adversarial attacks. This paper presents a new method based on a generative adversarial network (GAN) designed to mitigate the effects of such attacks on AMC systems. The proposed approach can recover the normal functioning of AMC models that have been sabotaged by attackers utilizing spectral or temporal manipulation. Furthermore, the method integrates an AMC model into a framework capable of producing defensive models that can accurately classify modulation types and resist adversarial attacks. Experimental evaluations on multiple classes of modulation using the RADAR-2000 based wireless test bed demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed defense mechanism. Our results indicate that the attacked models show a significant decline in accuracy, ranging from 31% to 65% for different classes, whereas the defensive models recover their normal performance, achieving accuracy above 95% for all tested classes. This method also showcases the general applicability to diverse adversarial attacks. Additionally, the defensive models exhibit robustness in real-world scenarios and can classify modulation types under non-malicious conditions, such as with signal loss or noise interference. The experimental research found the defensive models to be resilient even when signal strength is reduced to -10 dB, showing little decrease in accuracy, and can classify modulation types accurately even in the presence of moderate noise. The research applied five distinct types of adversarial attacks on the AMC model, including deep convolutional neural network based approaches, and revealed that the proposed framework can effectively counter both spectral and temporal adversarial attacks by achieving accuracy above 95% for all classes. The experimental findings also show that the proposed framework can effectively counter attacks implemented via wireless channels by achieving accuracy above 95% for all classes. The research concluded that the proposed framework can effectively counter four types of adversarial attacks, including those applied via wireless channels, noise, weak signal, and adversarial attacks, and can achieve accuracy above 95% for all classes. The results obtained from the real-world test bed demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach in enhancing the robustness of AMC models against adversarial attacks. The research highlights the potential applications of the proposed framework in diverse areas, such as aiding the design of AMC models, detecting adversarial attacks in real-time, and improving the robustness of communication systems. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of the parent cloud and its substructure.  The data used in this analysis consist of 11 samples with a wide mass spectrum, spanning from 10 to 5000 M_\
odot, and were obtained through community access to the Submillimeter Telescope Array Receiver Laboratory.  The data were then complemented by mass estimates obtained through radiative transfer models and by employing the empirical mass-to-temperature relationship developed by Kauffmann et al. (2017).  The resulting measurements yield a mass offset of approximately 0.5 deuterium-based solar masses between protostellar and starless cores, with an estimated uncertainty of 0.1 M_\
odot.  The data suggest that massive cores are primarily composed of a population of low-mass cores whose number density increases with distance.  Finally, our discovery could have far-reaching implications for the study of massive star formation, as it suggests the need for an alternative theory that does not rely on the established paradigm of massive prestellar core formation.  Further research, including data obtained via large surveys, is necessary to further explore this interesting finding. This paper investigates a complex problem where we need to assess the impact of adding items to a collection. The inherent nature of this problem prevents us from making absolute preferences between options, which prompts the use of context-dependent preference modeling. To tackle this issue, we examine two distinct Siamese network designs, contrasting one that compares the resultant collections after an addition with another that considers each item's individual contribution to the existing collection. Through experiments involving a real-world task of learning Magic: The Gathering deck-building card preferences, we found that the triplet network outperformed its counterpart and surpassed previous performance levels in this area. Additionally, our analysis reveals the benefits of utilizing triplet-ngram hard mining, a technique that enhances the effectiveness of our proposed network. The research demonstrates that the triplet network is more suitable for this particular task due to its ability to capture complex interactions between preferences. Furthermore, our findings suggest that leveraging the capabilities of deep neural networks can be valuable in identifying expert players within online communities, such as Magic: The Gathering. The proposed approach is versatile and can be applied to other preference-based ranking tasks across various domains. It is worth noting that, although our method outperforms existing solutions, which rely on pairwise learning, the gap in performance is relatively minor, and further research is needed to fully explore the use of triplet learning for preference-based ranking applications. Unlike previous studies that relied on psycholinguistic tools, our research delves into types of negation from developmental psychology. We examine this knowledge gap through a natural language inference task by creating a set of specialized questions from existing NLI datasets, which helps us assess a range of models' ability to process these negation types. Our analysis indicates models perform notably well on some negation categories, revealing a significant link between these categories and the models' capacity to understand causality and temporality. Notably, our findings suggest that models perform better on static causality types than human types, which raises important considerations. Moreover, our research shows that models excel on types involving explicit negation, but struggle with implicit negation types. Ultimately, our work highlights the importance of incorporating negation knowledge from developmental psychology into natural language processing to create more informed and transparent NLI datasets. By doing so, we take a crucial step towards developing more humane AI systems. The proposed dataset can be found at https://github.com/laurakiezow/NeGI-FiT.

Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing techniques to explain these models can be particularly challenging. To address this issue, a framework called LaViSE is proposed to enable convolutional neural networks to describe their internal workings in plain text. By using generic image data, this approach creates a link between visual and semantic information, allowing for its application across different domains without explicit labels. The LaViSE framework has a flexible structure, making it possible to analyze any network, regardless of whether its training data is accessible. Moreover, this technique can produce new explanations that go beyond the categories initially learned during training. It also has a significant application in discovering biases within datasets without needing additional labels. To facilitate further research, the framework, datasets, and code are openly available. Along with this, a new method called LaViSE-G for generating object-specific descriptors with a high level of semantic detail is introduced. It leverages generic image data to create a connection between visual and semantic information, and we demonstrate that this technique can be used to create explanations based on generic concepts, such as 'food' or 'large animal,' that are relevant to specific object categories. Furthermore, this method can be used to create explanations based on complex scenes without labels by training LaViSE-G on a variety of LaViSE-trained models and combining the generated descriptions. Developing a simplified microscopic model of cuprates is crucial in uncovering the mechanism behind high-temperature superconductivity. By comparing our simulation results with a recent photoemission spectroscopy study of one-dimensional cuprate chains, we have discovered that long-range electron-phonon coupling, which goes beyond standard models, significantly affects the interaction between neighboring electrons. Within reasonable limits of this interaction and phonon frequency, we have observed a strong attraction between neighboring electrons, which is consistent with experimental observations. Additionally, we have found that the interaction between neighboring electrons is influenced by the structural and chemical properties shared by one-dimensional and two-dimensional cuprate materials. This simplified model, taking into account long-range electron-phonon coupling, provides a new and important perspective on cuprate high-temperature superconductivity and associated quantum phenomena. Further research is needed to evaluate the relevance of this finding to the full cuprate system.

The ongoing Population-based HIV Impact Assessment project aims to measure national and regional progress in combating the HIV epidemic, a primary goal of UNAIDS' 90-90-90 targets. By analyzing data from high-risk countries in sub-Saharan Africa, researchers hope to gain a deeper understanding of the key factors driving the epidemic. This study proposes a novel causal learning approach to identify crucial indicators and causal links related to the 90-90-90 targets. This method preserves critical information about key factors, in contrast to existing approaches which often result in significant data loss. When applied to the Malawi HIV assessment data set, it produced notable results, highlighting the importance of factors like age, condom usage, and proximity to HIV care facilities in reducing HIV transmission. Through comparisons using the Bayesian Information Criterion and Monte Carlo simulations, it was demonstrated that this new approach achieves better data utilization and accurately measures the relevance of indicators and causal links, outperforming existing methods. Furthermore, it was found that this approach identified a key factor associated with female HIV awareness as education level and with male awareness as proximity to HIV care facilities. By providing a conservative data estimation of prevalence that meets UNAIDS' accuracy requirements, it was established that the estimated 90-90-90 targets for Malawi are achievable under specific prevalence estimations. This study suggests that advanced causal learning can effectively inform public health policy by identifying crucial indicators, causal links, and critical factors driving the national HIV epidemic. The equilibrium problem described by the Nikaid\^o-Isoda-Fan inequality encompasses several key problems like optimization, variational inequality, and others, as specific instances. This paper aims to provide a clear outline illustrating the connection between fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping and solutions to the equilibrium problem that satisfy particular monotonicity and Lipschitz-type constraints. It also proposes and examines two iteration schemes for approximating equilibrium problems and their respective fixed-point sets, enabling the establishment of full convergence for appropriate conditions and even convergence to the smallest equilibrium solution for additional, stricter requirements. The schemes have the additional benefit of enabling decomposition and analytical calculation for problems whose subdifferential mappings can be easily computed. As a result, various important special cases like optimization and variational inequality are brought within computational reach through the proposed algorithms. Moreover, we have verified the flexibility of these schemes by applying them to some meaningful real-world problems. These include a problem of convex optimization and a particular nuclear norm minimization problem arising in signal processing, which we have solved numerically in this paper. It is worth noting that the fixed-point convergence of the Moreau proximal mapping based algorithms for equilibrium problems has not been explored before, and this work, therefore, represents an important contribution in this area. These algorithms have also been shown to be equivalent to certain split convex programming algorithms that can also be used for analyzing the convergence of the aforementioned problems as special cases. For instance, fixed-point convergence can be established for the split convex programming algorithm for solving the ill-posed problem of convex convex optimization, for particular monotone hessian and Lipschitz-type constraints. These algorithms have also been shown to encompass famous algorithms like the Krasnoselskii-Mann and the extra-gradient methods, which are widely known for their effectiveness in solving equilibrium and variational problems as well as convex optimization. The debate on turbulent effects influencing magnetic activity in the Sun and stars persists. The mean-field theory provides a widely applied framework to link these effects to fundamental magnetohydrodynamics, although it's not possible to observe these effects directly. To gain insight, researchers utilize global convective dynamo simulations to investigate turbulent effects, which are measured by using the test-field method to calculate transport coefficients based on the mean-field framework. This study found these coefficients to deviate from their predicted values under the Taylor hypothesis, causing overestimation of alpha-effect and underestimation of beta-effect when using the fast-rotating approximation. It was found alpha coefficient to be 40% higher than estimated values when using Taylor hypothesis, and beta coefficient to be 40% lower than estimated values when using Taylor hypothesis, this in turn affects the shape of the alpha-coefficient's differential rotation profile. The reason for these discrepancies with the Taylor hypothesis lies with the reorganization of coherent eddies, this in turn causes the beta-effect to be related to the reorganization of these eddies rather than simply being determined by the angular velocity gradient, this in turn makes the beta-effect to be non-zero at the equator and in turn to be dependent on the magnetic Rossby number. The researchers propose the use of the fast-rotating approximation based on the mean-field theory to be inaccurate and in turn to be contributing to errors when simulating solar and stellar convective dynamos, this in turn may cause the overestimation of the growth rates in these systems and in turn to lead to an early onset of the dynamo compared to what is observed in reality. To further quantify these discrepancies, the researchers used the total energy balance in the simulations to calculate the relative errors in the simulated growth rates when using the mean-field theory and in turn to determine the accuracy of the theory. The researchers found the relative errors in the simulated growth rates to be as high as 60% when using the mean-field theory, this in turn highlights the need for an improved and more accurate theoretical framework for describing and predicting turbulent effects that affect magnetohydrodynamics in the Sun and stars. The researchers propose one-way lagrangian holographic modeling as a promising approach to enable the prediction of these effects and in turn to improve simulations of the Sun and stars. We observed that the outflows' velocities did not exceed the galaxy's rotational velocity, causing the gas to be deflected toward the edges by the disk's curvature. A simplified version of the original Vlasov-Maxwell equations for magnetized plasmas is provided by quasilinear theory, which describes how particles interact with waves through resonant processes. The reduced model in a turbulent plasma setting shows how a broad distribution of particles can give rise to spectral energy densities, which in turn affect the wave dynamics. The approach is applied to a magnetic mirror trap, where it is demonstrated that the simplified theory is sufficient for understanding energy and particle transport, but for other aspects, such as the statistical behavior of trapped particles, a return to the full Vlasov-Maxwell equations is necessary. The equations are solved in the trap using a Hamiltonian method based on four-field theory, which is characterized by phase space interfaces and discontinuous solutions. The solution is constructed using a Lagrangian formulation and four-current analysis, which yields precise and often analytic results for the four-field structure. The approach is capable of handling complex problems in magnetized plasmas, from shock formation to phase space mixing and particle confinement. The theory of turbulence in the magnetic mirror trap reveals a broader applicability of singularity formation and phase space mixing, which is supported by simulations and comparisons with original test particle results. Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis. In these tests, we found that variable stepsize SGLMs are especially advantageous on grids generated by geometric sequences, and we present an initial set of conditions for higher order methods, although these do not yet generalize to order four. Nonetheless, our results indicate the significant potential of SGLMs with adaptive step sizes, which could be particularly beneficial in non-linear stability investigations, such as the numerical integration of Symplectic Hamiltonian systems, although this application is left for future exploration. We provide a relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T and solutions of a specific Lyapunov inequality in B+(X,X*), where X is a Banach space. The Lyapunov inequality solutions' exponential growth rate directly correlates with the exponential stability rate of T. This relationship's consequence shows that if certain solutions of the Lyapunov inequality are not exponentially growing, then T is exponentially stable. The relationship established here also applies to approximate methods, like the Picard, Crank-Nicolson, and Galerkin methods, enabling us to assess the approximate temporal exponential stability of time-varying inhomogeneous differential equations. Furthermore, understanding this relationship leads to a straightforward proof of a classic theorem by Russell that addresses approximate stability of the equation u't = A(t)u with boundary conditions u(x,0) in a subset of the boundary of X. Since regularity of solutions is not a requirement, our approach is considered an enhancement over existing general methods for establishing stability inequalities. We demonstrate the usefulness of our findings by applying them to a model based on an oscillating string and a mass moving on it. We derive both the necessary and sufficient condition for the exact and a corresponding estimate for the approximate temporal exponential stability of the model, as well as gaining insight into the relationship between regularity of solutions and the approximate stability. For instance, in the case of a non-regular solution, we demonstrate that the Picard method yields a stable approximation, whereas a method based on the finite element technique applied in reverse time may not. We extend the presented approach to establish a correspondence between the Lyapunov inequality and a specific maximal regularity of the resolvent of A in B(X,X*), where A is a closed, densely defined operator in X. This correspondence is then applied to study the maximal regularity and exponential stability of the resolvent of a time-varying inhomogeneous Cauchy problem u't = A(t)u with boundary conditions u(x,0) in a subset of the boundary of X. We show that if the resolvent solutions' growth rate does not exceed the exponential stability rate of T, then a correspondence exists between the Lyapunov inequality solutions' growth rate and the resolvent solutions' growth rate. This correspondence is then applied to study the regularity of the resolvent of a time-varying inhomogeneous boundary value problem of a model based on a classical vibration model of a string. Portfolio managers assess investment success in relation to market standards, specifically using the Standard & Poor 500 index as a benchmark. Our revised assessment combines two key measures: the portfolio's absolute value and its performance relative to that of a chosen benchmark. The traditional Merton problem, however, solely focuses on the portfolio's absolute wealth. In contrast, our proposed model encompasses both absolute and relative wealth in a comprehensive utility function. The utility functions, derived from power law equations, allow for flexibility with varying exponents to suit individual benchmarks or market scenarios. The outcome provides an explicit solution and is compared to the original Merton problem solution, with implications for the Capital Asset Pricing Model framework. The conventional solution, though optimal, is inherently unstable; in contrast, our solution offers a more stable investment approach, resulting in a lower maximum utility compared to the Merton problem solution. The difference in wealth between the two solutions, calculated as the relative wealth plus the absolute wealth, is also analyzed and compared. The findings suggest that, in the optimal investment strategy identified, the portfolio typically allocates a significant portion, often over 90%, to the absolute wealth optimization solution. Consequently, investors may experience substantial losses if the market performs poorly, thereby failing to achieve a maximum utility, highlighting the inherent flaws in the Merton problem solution. The trade-off between absolute and relative wealth optimizations is then examined through the solution difference's dependence on the exponents, time horizon, and market returns. The behavior of the utility functions and their derivatives are analyzed, discussed, and compared to the Merton problem solution. The solution difference's growth rate is determined and analyzed, resulting in a maximum growth phase followed by a decay back to a stable, optimal growth rate, thus indicating the stable nature of the optimal investment strategy. The most abundant galaxy type in the cosmos is dwarf galaxies, which exhibit distinct characteristics when compared to larger, brighter counterparts. This article centers on the physical and chemical properties of the interstellar material within dwarf galaxies containing notable quantities of gas and dust. The discussion includes the characteristics of neutral and ionized gases, the effects of dust, and initial evidence suggesting the presence of active nuclei in these galaxies. The article also considers the cosmological implications of primordial helium abundance and the similarity between local Green Pea galaxies and younger, proto-galactic systems in the early universe. The discussion concludes by highlighting the significance of dwarf galaxies in the study of galaxy evolution and the cosmos. The article draws together information from existing research while also suggesting future areas for investigation worthy of exploration. The content has been made available for free and is suitable for undergraduate students pursuing degrees in astronomy, astrophysics, and related fields. The first six chapters focus on the composition of the interstellar material while the final three explores the cosmological implications of the findings. We examine the preservation of single-particle excitations in a strongly correlated electronic system influenced by both electron and hole excitations. To achieve this, we utilize an extended version of the Anderson model that accounts for both electrons and holes as a fermionic bath. A semi-circular fermionic bath with temperature parameters calibrated to match the electron and hole baths yields an optimal configuration in which both the electron and hole baths align with the Anderson model's parameters without disrupting the preservation of single-particle excitations. As an alternative, we investigate the impact of both electron and hole baths on the Anderson model's single-particle excitation energy in the strong correlation regime, finding that a wide range of hole excitation levels can maintain approximately $\sim$10% stability in single-particle excitations. Furthermore, we observe that a 100% level of both electron and hole excitations still permits $\sim$5% stability in single-particle excitations. The proposed method is applicable to both unitary and orthogonal symmetry classes. Additionally, we compare and contrast our results with those obtained through diagrammatic calculations, identifying some discrepancies. Utilizing crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk to acquire top-tier human annotations proves more complicated than initially thought, influenced by several key factors, such as task instructions and annotator compensation, among others. To prevent inaccurate annotations which could mislead automatic summarization systems, we develop a multi-stage recruitment process targeting high-quality MTurk workers. By establishing a rigorous evaluation pipeline, we demonstrate the ability to exclude unskilled workers before evaluation tasks are initiated, and measure the resulting quality using both source-based and sample-based assessment methods. Specifically, we evaluate summization performance on 1,125 documents from seven diverse sources across seven crowdsourcing tasks using the F-score metric. We discover that source-based evaluation overestimates human performance due to the nature of source documents, whereas sample-based evaluation demonstrates that even experienced MTurk workers fail to reach typical annotation quality benchmarks. To address this, we develop instruction modifications aimed at improving annotator efficiency and incorporate additional filters to eliminate unskilled workers. Consequently, our investigation yields a satisfactory F-score of 0.309 despite the inherent difficulties, costs, and limitations associated with human annotations. Notably, the related summization errors explain merely 1% of incorrect annotations, underscoring the significance of high-quality human annotations in the summization process. The study also offers guidance for summization evaluation and provides a resource for future evaluation pipelines. The project's source code, pre-annotated datasets, and summization evaluation tools are available at https://github.com/automatisoft/MEGAN. As an added contribution, we release pre-annotated datasets for seven news sources, comprising 1.085.830 comments gathered from 2015 to 2017, spanning the U.S. presidential primaries and the European migrant crisis. Additionally, we provide summization examples for one of these sources, the Huffington Post, at https://huffpost-insumm.meinanalytics.com. We hope this initiative fosters collaboration and facilitates the sharing of evaluation pipeline components to ensure reproducibility and improve summization performance. Furthermore, the experience gained from this study may facilitate the adaptation of our evaluation pipeline to other complex annotation tasks. By quantifying the percentage recovery over the baseline for a range of potential applications, we aim to offer an efficient method for evaluating summization progress across various contexts. Ultimately, the research outlines potential avenues to further enhance the quality of human annotations for the purpose of automatic summization. Text-video retrieval, an essential task of practical importance, has seen escalating interest in recent years. Most current approaches focus on learning temporal and linguistic representations from video and text data, then combining them for final joint representation generation. Nevertheless, these methods fail to harness the full potential of token-level information in both inputs. This paper proposes TS2-Net, a cutting-edge token shift module that effectively transfers token-level information from one modality to the other. We incorporate TS2-Net into a transformer-based cross-modal encoder, allowing it to capture shifts of tokens within videos under the guidance of text descriptions. This enables more refined video-text matching and enhanced retrieval performance as a result. Our method outperforms the state-of-the-art models on both ActivityNet and VATEX benchmarks, with significant improvements of 11.8% and 15.4% for top 1 recall, respectively. We also substantially reduce training costs by 65%. Our project's code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/minds-ai/TS2-Net. This research was supported by a gift from Mind's Eye Technologies. We would like to extend our gratitude to Ming-Ching Chang, Yi-Hao Hong, and Hsiang-Rui Chang for their invaluable guidance and assistance. We are proud to announce that TS2-Net won the first place prize at the ActivityNet 2.0 challenge in 2019. Our team's work significantly surpasses the results achieved by Li et al. in 2020, a paper we were inspired by. This work further advances the state-of-the-art on VATEX by a margin of 15.4% for top 1 recall, outperforming the best previous model in the field. We believe our findings notably reveal the TS2-Net module's capability to leverage shifts of tokens within videos under the guidance of text descriptions for more refined video-text matching and enhanced retrieval performance. We are confident that this work opens the door to a variety of token-level knowledge transfer methods across different cross-modal tasks. Our method's training and testing code, as well as the trained models, can be found at https://github.com/minds-ai/TS2-Net. This research was supported by a gift from Mind's Eye Technologies. We would like to extend our gratitude to Ming-Ching Chang, Yi-Hao Hong, and Hsiang-Rui Chang for their invaluable guidance and assistance. The intricate connection between many-body interactions and the spatial dimension of a system plays a pivotal role in various quantum phenomena that emerge from these interactions. A compelling example of this relationship is the way a Bose gas thermalizes when its dimensions are reduced to one through confinement. This process, implemented experimentally using optical lattices, is found to have far-reaching consequences at the phase transition point, with the system's complexity increasing significantly when it loses one dimension. Furthermore, our research reveals that this many-body interaction becomes highly entangled, with the entanglement density exhibiting a maximum at the center of this thermalization phase transition. This level of interaction can be quantified by measuring the total correlation entropy within the system and is comparable to entanglement found in one-dimensional systems. Importantly, our statistical analysis shows that this interaction can be attributed to individual particles rather than collections of them. Lastly, our phase diagram illustrates that adding more particles' weakly scattered waves can drive the system away from one-dimensional behavior, causing it to re-enter a phase where the system is well-defined locally but appears disordered on a larger scale when measured. This research is primarily based on simulations in a context-free environment, though it has relevance for 1D to 2D phase transitions observed in the study of Bose gases, such as in studies of quark-gluon plasmas, cold atoms, and other similar systems. This study's concepts also find applications in the phenomenon of dark solitons found in Bose-Einstein condensates. It is expected that a similar relationship will be observed in other types of quantum systems that involve both wave-particle interactions and phase transitions. Refer to the report provided for further details. 

Key words - correlation entropy, entanglement, Bose gas, dark solitons, phase transitions.

To utilize contemporary computing systems efficiently, an important consideration is reducing the communication cost associated with data transfer, especially when calculating the tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) in just a few data passes. The prevailing subspace randomized methods used to compute the t-SVD require 2q + 2 passes over the tensor data, where q represents a positive integer variable for iteration refinement. In this work, we introduce a new family of randomized t-SVD algorithms employing a novel data partitioning strategy based on tensor standard parallel canonical decomposition. The proposed approach yields a 0(eps^-2 (n_{\tau}n_{\nu}) / q) matrix factorization with 2q passes, which refines the approximation quality and minimizes data transfer at each pass. The proposed algorithm's efficacy has been demonstrated in several applications utilizing tensors. We present a benchmark comparison between the presented method and existing t-SVD methods, illustrating its advantages in terms of data transfer efficiency, especially in the approximate t-SVD setting with a given tolerance level. Furthermore, we provide error bounds for the computed t-SVD matrix factorization and examine the effect of refined iterations on the approximation error. The proposed algorithm's implementation is available online at the URL https://github.com/jmvega1/tensor-svd-rf. The results illustrate the practical benefits of the new algorithm, showcasing its performance in the approximate mode with a fixed tolerance and reduced data transfer cost. In the exact mode, both the proposed method and current best techniques achieve similar high-quality matrix factorization with q approaching infinity. Based on these outcomes, we recommend the proposed algorithm as an open-source solution for the community. The software repository containing the implementation of this work, including a sample demonstration, is accessible via the provided URL. The investigation is focused on solving a boundary value equation, which is derived from the scalar curvature and Jacobian compatibility condition. The equation can be broken down into two parts - a Dirichlet boundary problem and a mean curvature equation. Initially, the study considers a subcritical approximation of the problem, which reveals the presence of multiple finite energy solutions displaying intriguing behavior such as concentration at multiple points on the boundary. Specifically, it focuses on a Poisson kernel as the underlying probability distribution, although the findings are capable of adapting to any smooth distribution. For this purpose, an approximation of the probability distribution's density function is initially created with an additive error analysis, and subsequently, the probability that a random $d$-dimensional excursion surface includes a specific topological feature is determined. Subsequently, the overall probability of containing this feature is calculated through an integral representation, which can also be transformed into an additive formula with an additive error involving the probability distribution's density function. The approach is illustrated by generating simulated data and examining the distribution of Betti numbers in random surfaces. Furthermore, it allows for a data-driven estimation of the total probability associated with general excursion patterns, and reveals the inherent limitations of estimating the lower-dimensional components of a randomly sampled manifold. The method is applicable to any underlying probability distribution, and can be extended to analyze different types of topological features. The approach offers a straightforward technique for estimating the probability distribution of isomorphic excursions and provides a feasible solution for estimating Betti numbers of rare events, thereby facilitating a more accurate estimation of sparse data manifolds. The study also addresses potential applications and implications of the theoretical findings, including the estimation of rare limits in sparse datasets. The work has been made publicly available through an online repository containing all the implementation details and data visualizations required to reproduce the research's content and has included a discussion on various future extension opportunities. The approach has been extended to analyze non-Poisson distributions in additional studies, and further develops this concept through a theoretical analysis of random geometric patterns in higher-dimensional spaces. The research's findings have been applied to two real-world scenarios, including the estimation of rare limits in $z$-score analysis of simulated functional magnetic resonance imaging data and the examination of simulated random geometric patterns in a neutron detection system. The approach provides a feasible solution for estimating Betti numbers under general excursion patterns and can be used to calculate the probability distribution of isomorphic excursions and general homology excursions. The study concludes by outlining the existing limitations and potential future extension opportunities for the proposed research and highlights an open conjecture regarding the estimation of Betti numbers involving general excursion patterns which remains unaddressed in current literature. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing the performance of three approaches: one relying on 2D object detection and another using 2.5D predictions along with depth information to estimate camera pose, against traditional methods. Unanticipated changes in the simulation environment and object geometry were introduced to assess the robustness of the models. Our results indicate that artificial intelligence-based methods surpass traditional calibration techniques, with specific adaptation and extension of the 2D object detection method yielding the best results, although this came at the expense of greater simulation complexity. Our findings suggest that these methods are highly sensitive to the diversity of the training data, highlighting the need for advanced methods to deal with novel objects and settings encountered during execution. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/tatianaflores/mapc-camkalib. Our contributions lie in the development of multiple deep learning approaches for real-time calibration of an eye-in-hand camera in a purely simulated environment. Our codes may facilitate the quick implementation of these techniques in actual systems. Our research also sheds light on their main limitations, mainly their dependence on diverse and representative data, like any machine learning approach. These issues could be addressed by developing new methods or implementing techniques to increase the learning data's coverage. Our work utilizes only a single color image for calibration, unlike approaches that also utilize information about the object's geometry or previous data to calculate the camera's position, making our methods more practical in scenarios where this information is unavailable or known with low precision. Our simulations involve a dynamic environment with moving objects and changing light conditions to calculate the camera's pose in a variety of scenarios. Our models demonstrate their ability to calculate the camera's position in the current frame and predict its position in the next frame with good accuracy, although their performance diminishes when the object's geometry changes. In real-world settings, RL systems face difficulties due to various constraints that are challenging to formalize mathematically. For RL applications, it is crucial that agents can detect and adapt to these constraints to ensure safe decision-making. This study investigates the issue of inferring constraints from observational data of an agent's compliant behavior. Experimental validation is performed to verify that the proposed method successfully identifies the most relevant constraints an agent is expected to follow. Furthermore, these constraints can be generalized and applied to novel agents with different structures and reward schemes. In contrast to existing methods that are primarily designed for tabular settings, specific types of constraints, or assume environment dynamics, the presented framework can autonomously learn any type of Markovian constraint within complex high-dimensional environments without the need for model-based representations. This capability is successfully demonstrated through a series of applications, including learning an agent's capacity to navigate an discrete grid-based space. The theoretical framework, along with the associated implementation, is made accessible through an online repository at https://github.com/myusof/rlcen. This research reveals that the enforced constraints can be diverse in nature, such as avoiding cycles, preventing policies with high trajectory cross-entropy, or other constraint profiles that are dependent on the particular problem at hand. For example, the learned constraints of an agent that is trained to perform at MaxEnt-I explores the possibility of an agent's bottom layer being composed of all states with zero probability, as a result of preventing policies with high trajectory cross-entropy. This means that this type of agent will inevitably visit states with higher probabilities as it progresses. On the other hand, the constraint profiles of an agent that is trained to perform at MaxEnt-I at the level of MaxEnt-I-II exhibit variation depending on their respective difficulties, indicating all zero probability states at lower levels and a trend towards including all states with the maximum probability at higher levels. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in inferring constraints that are both abstract and relevant to safe decision-making. The framework's capability to infer constraint profiles with various levels of granularity was observed, suggesting that the approach can be both a threat modeling and clarification resource for safety engineers to better comprehend the constraints an agent is expected to follow in various high-risk RL applications. This research aims to pave the way for the practical utilization of constraint learning in real-world RL settings. Additionally, our algorithm can compute an optimal vertex separator in $O(n)$ space when the treewidth is $O(m^{1/2-\epsilon})$, which outperforms existing space-efficient algorithms in this area. Similar to previous research, our algorithm relies on an algorithm for partitioning vertices around bounded treewidth graphs, and we have also developed an efficient version of the latter. A practical implementation of our approach has shown improved performance in storage needs, and we have also observed a decrease in the resolution of the approximated vertex separator when the $\epsilon$ value is decreased. Our algorithm is further described in terms of computational complexity, and we have found that reducing $\epsilon$ results in an increase in computational time but also leads to an improvement in the quality of the approximated vertex separator. Therefore, there appears to be a trade-off between computational efficiency and the quality of the output obtained. For instance, in the specific scenario of a grid graph with $400K$ vertices, reducing $\epsilon$ from $0.5$ to $0.1$ results in an almost $3.5$-fold improvement in the quality of the output but at the cost of increased computational and storage needs. A similar trade-off is also reported for graphs such as random trees and bipartite random graphs with a specific number of vertices. We have also used our algorithm to compute approximate vertex separators for specific problems, such as the facility location problem, and demonstrated how these can be utilized to solve restricted versions of the original input-only optimization problem more efficiently than an exact algorithm in this context. A substantial portion of network information comes from edge weights and their directionality.
Most current network measures only consider connections and ignore weights and edge orientation.
To fill this gap, we've developed new versions of the k-core algorithm that enable control over weight usage.
Our work focuses on fully-weighted clusters and hybrid approaches, which balance connectivity and weight impact.
Through theoretical analysis and computational experiments, we've found that fully-weighted methods are more suitable for multi-level and multi-type networks.
Additionally, we've modified the k-core algorithm to incorporate multi-level structures, leading to more accurate and efficient results in various network analyses. Further development of weighted clustering and k-core algorithms could have a significant impact on subsequent algorithms using coreness, community structure, and network topological features. As such, these improvements could facilitate novel insights and applications in multiple fields. The open-source implementation of our work is currently available online.

We established a non-asymptotic lower bound for the eigenvalues of a design matrix, generated by linear bandit algorithms that incur sub-linear regret in action spaces with consistent observations. This lower bound has a specific structure, involving the sum of functions that depend on the frequency of certain actions and the size of the action space, raised to a power that grows polynomially with the action space dimension. Consequently, this result implies that there are scenarios where even bandit algorithms that run in near-linear time can not avoid incurring regret that grows sub-linearly with the number of steps despite selecting signals optimally. Moreover, our finding can be viewed as an extension of a previous result by Bubeck et al. that established an upper bound for the eigenvalues of the design matrix, by removing certain assumptions that were necessary for that bound, thereby yielding a "sharp-down" result in this context. Furthermore, this result addresses an open question previously posed by Radev and Urai which focused on determining whether it was possible for any bandit algorithm to incur regret that grows sub-linearly with the number of steps even when the action space consistent observations are incurred at most once. Our finding hereby answers this question affirmatively by making three adjustments to that problem - it does not impose a limit on the number of consistent observations incurred per step, does not require the signals to be selected optimally, and does not impose general bounds on the regret to grow slower than the number of steps. Moreover, our result is based on a simpler characterization of action spaces that only requires the actions to be mapped to real numbers as opposed to a more general measure space. Our result does, however, come with an additional guarantee that the eigenvalues it provided will be bounded from above by a function that grows factorially with the action space dimension, implying a general trade-off between the amount of regret incurred and the amount of action space dimension incurred. Graphene with gaps has been proposed to showcase the valley Hall effect, where different types of electron flows are generated based on spin and orbital properties.  Our research, however, demonstrates that it's actually the orbital Hall effect that dominates in this setup, rather than the valley Hall effect, and can be controlled through the use of magnetic fields. Orbits with specific edge orientations and their opposite counterparts cancel each other out, resulting in distinct orbital Hall resistivities that are determined by specific magnetic field orientations. This distinction gives rise to various symmetry-based rules that govern the possible flows. Ultimately, specific parameters end up influencing the magnitude of these flows. Our study presents different scenarios in which these orbital Hall effects are observable in a nanoribbon model. We identify a unique phase where the effects are identical for both types of edges and are inversely proportional to the nanoribbon's width. Our work lays the foundation for distinguishing between the orbital Hall and valley Hall effects via a simple conductivity test. Generally, the former is characterized by a linear relationship between conductivity and magnetic field strength, whereas the latter displays an inverse and linear relationship, respectively. Our study reveals the prominence of orbital Hall effects in gapped graphene nanoribbons. The process of matching objects between photometric catalogs can lead to inaccuracies when objects of different brightness are mistaken for the same source. However, incorporating the magnitudes of sources can rectify this issue and improve accuracy. A novel approach described here utilizes photometric data from multiple catalogs to enhance the counterpart-matching process, leading to a substantial improvement in the assessment of matches. By including this photometric information, prior astrophysical knowledge can be omitted from the assessment, offering increased flexibility. Furthermore, this method accounts for the possibility that some sources have no counterparts or multiple potential matches. A detailed description of the method's underlying probability calculations is provided, incorporating systematic astrometric effects. Two test cases demonstrate the method's effectiveness in matching IPHAS-Gaia, IPHAS, and 2MASS catalogs, showcasing its versatility when dealing with various data sets of different wavelength coverages and astrometric precisions. The importance of incorporating magnitude information in the assessment of matches is highlighted in both cases. Moreover, the method's potential for use in the analysis of various astrophysical sources is discussed. Available online at https://www.u-aastronomy.ca/, the method's software can be readily applied to various astrophysical sources. A companion paper explores the application of this method in identifying potential counterparts of transients across multiple photometric catalogs. Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected concepts. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly balance the exploration of all concept relationships and large hierarchical structures. OntoPlot's novel hybrid visualisation incorporates icicle plots, interactive elements, and space-efficient visual compression to enhance understanding and reduce visual clutter. Through a user study involving domain experts, we compared OntoPlot's usability to that of Protégé, the industry-standard ontology editor, finding that OntoPlot surpassed expectations in facilitating association-related tasks and earned widespread endorsement from domain specialists. Furthermore, OntoPlot received the first-place prize at Visualizing Data 2021. The developed software is open-source and accessible at https://ontoplot.github.io. We encourage stakeholders to utilise OntoPlot in hypergraph-based visualisation, recommending a gradual, semi-automated approach to adding associations and introducing a novel 'dendritic' OntoPlot layout, termed OCL. OCL is still in its preliminary stage and requires refinement, and we propose HyperPlot as a general framework for visualising hypergraphs, opening up new possibilities for hypergraph-based OntoPlot systems. Ultimately, OntoPlot has the potential to revolutionise the visualisation and exploration of vast, complex knowledge domains, benefiting fields like biology, medicine, and beyond. The software is open-source and accessible at https://ontoplot.github.io. We encourage stakeholders to utilise OntoPlot in a controlled manner to assess its efficacy in a hypergraph-based visualisation in a subsequent large-scale user study. The resulting system could serve as an invaluable tool for understanding complex knowledge domains and facilitating faster, more accurate downstream analyses. We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to facilitate semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss aims to derive a common speech-text representation through a shared neural network, whereas CycleGAN leverages cycle-consistency and identity mapping to preserve input characteristics after cross-domain conversion. As both approaches can train end-to-end models with unpaired data, we leverage their strengths to improve the speech-text mapping and shared representation, ultimately enhancing speech-to-text performance. Our experimental findings reveal that this novel approach yields significant reductions in character error rate (CAR or CER) across a diverse range of low-resource scenarios. For example, we observe CER decreases of 8.45% and 3.65% on the WSJ resource when limited to 1 second of speech feature input and unbalanced data distributions, respectively. Our method also significantly outperforms controlled training with unpaired data, indicating its potential as a versatile solution for low-resource and real-world speech-to-text tasks. C code for this research is available at https://github.com/gridsunny/ddd-sfsr, showcasing its ease of use and adaptability. Additionally, we present a new CER metric that normalizes based on sentence length to provide a more accurate sense of the recognition performance's progress during training. Our findings suggest that this type of length-based normalization leads to generally lower CER values compared to the traditional 5-gram normalized approach. We hypothesize that this advantage may result from the sentence length normalization's sensitivity to the dataset's sentence length distribution, which is a characteristic that differs across various data sets and could work in their favor. Furthermore, we observe that this type of length-based normalization in CER is not suitable for evaluating progress within a learning system, as it is an after-effects metric that is not influenced by the model's predictions. In contrast, we present a new metric called WER-CER, a correlation-based measure that aims to evaluate models of this type in a more unbiased manner. As an alternative to the traditional metric, WER-CER is based on the weighted average of WER and CER, with the weights assigned based on the characteristic sentence length of the data. We observe that this type of metric choice is not crucial and that both metrics capable of capturing valuable information regarding the model's performance.
